sections.title: Cancer Chemotherapy & Targeted Therapy
subsections: Mitotic inhibitors, antibiotics and topoisomerase agents

entries.mechanism: Reversibly inhibits COX-1 and COX-2, reducing prostaglandin synthesis — less pain, inflammation and fever.
entries.uses: Mild-to-moderate pain, musculoskeletal injury, fever, dysmenorrhoea; IV form closes patent ductus arteriosus.
entries.cautions: GI irritation and ulceration; renal impairment and fluid retention; may worsen asthma. “Triple whammy” AKI with ACEi plus diuretic.

entries.mechanism: As ibuprofen; longer half-life allows twice-daily dosing.
entries.uses: Chronic inflammatory pain, arthritis, acute gout, dysmenorrhoea.
entries.cautions: Same GI/renal/asthma profile; comparatively lower cardiovascular risk than other NSAIDs.

entries.mechanism: Potent non-selective COX inhibition with relative COX-2 preference.
entries.uses: Musculoskeletal and post-operative pain; topical gel for local joint pain.
entries.cautions: Highest cardiovascular thrombotic risk of the traditional NSAIDs; avoid in ischaemic heart disease.

entries.mechanism: Very potent COX inhibitor; closes the ductus arteriosus by removing prostaglandin support.
entries.uses: Acute gout, ankylosing spondylitis, patent ductus arteriosus in neonates.
entries.cautions: Marked GI toxicity and CNS effects (headache, confusion); one of the harsher NSAIDs.

entries.mechanism: Strong peripheral COX inhibition giving opioid-sparing analgesia.
entries.uses: Short-term severe post-operative pain.
entries.cautions: High GI and bleeding risk; use limited to a few days only.

entries.mechanism: COX inhibition with some prostaglandin-receptor antagonism.
entries.uses: Dysmenorrhoea, menorrhagia.
entries.cautions: Diarrhoea; seizures in overdose.

entries.mechanism: Long-acting non-selective COX inhibition.
entries.uses: Chronic arthritis where once-daily dosing helps.
entries.cautions: Long half-life prolongs GI exposure; serious skin reactions.

entries.mechanism: Preferentially inhibits COX-2 at lower doses.
entries.uses: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis.
entries.cautions: Selectivity is lost at higher doses — GI risk returns.

entries.mechanism: Converted in liver to an active COX inhibitor; relatively gastric-sparing as the parent is non-acidic.
entries.uses: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis.
entries.cautions: Standard NSAID cautions; long half-life.

entries.mechanism: Irreversibly acetylates COX. In anucleate platelets this disables thromboxane A2 for the platelet's 7–10 day lifespan — duration decoupled from half-life.
entries.uses: Low dose: secondary prevention of MI and stroke. High dose: pain and fever (now rare); Kawasaki disease.
entries.cautions: GI bleeding; Reye's syndrome — never under 16 during viral illness; caution in asthma. Overdose: tinnitus, mixed acid-base disturbance.

entries.mechanism: Selectively inhibits inducible COX-2, sparing gastroprotective COX-1.
entries.uses: Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis where GI risk is a concern.
entries.cautions: Fewer ulcers, but shifting the vascular prostaglandin balance raises thrombotic risk — a trade-off, not an upgrade.

entries.mechanism: As celecoxib, longer acting.
entries.uses: Arthritis, acute gout.
entries.cautions: Hypertension and cardiovascular risk; avoid in uncontrolled BP.

entries.mechanism: Mechanism not fully established — weak central COX effect plus other central actions; little peripheral anti-inflammatory activity.
entries.uses: First-line for mild-to-moderate pain and fever at all ages, including pregnancy.
entries.cautions: Very safe at correct dose; in overdose NAPQI exhausts glutathione and destroys hepatocytes. Antidote: acetylcysteine. Patient may feel well for a day before liver failure declares.

entries.mechanism: Inhibits monoamine reuptake and modulates central pain pathways.
entries.uses: Moderate pain where opioids and NSAIDs are unsuitable.
entries.cautions: Anticholinergic effects, sweating, tachycardia; avoid in convulsive disorders.

entries.mechanism: Barbiturate sedation combined with a simple analgesic.
entries.uses: Tension-type headache (largely US practice).
entries.cautions: Dependence and medication-overuse headache; barbiturate withdrawal on stopping.

entries.mechanism: Only ~10% is converted by CYP2D6 into morphine, its active form — hence highly variable response.
entries.uses: Mild-to-moderate pain; cough suppression; antidiarrhoeal.
entries.cautions: Constipation, nausea, drowsiness. Poor metabolisers get no relief; ultra-rapid metabolisers reach dangerous morphine levels. Avoid post-tonsillectomy in children.

entries.mechanism: Mu-agonist, active without CYP2D6 activation.
entries.uses: Moderate pain where codeine response is unreliable.
entries.cautions: Standard opioid profile; accumulates in renal impairment.

entries.mechanism: Weak mu-agonist that also inhibits serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake — a second, monoamine pain pathway.
entries.uses: Moderate pain where a pure opioid is undesirable.
entries.cautions: Serotonin syndrome risk (poor choice with an SSRI); lowers seizure threshold; CYP2D6-dependent activation.

entries.mechanism: Mu-agonist plus noradrenaline reuptake inhibition; no active metabolite.
entries.uses: Moderate-to-severe pain, including neuropathic.
entries.cautions: Less serotonergic than tramadol but still lowers seizure threshold.

entries.mechanism: Full agonist at mu-opioid receptors — powerful analgesia, with euphoria, sedation, respiratory depression, constipation and miosis as inescapable companions.
entries.uses: Severe pain — post-operative, trauma, MI, cancer and palliative care; acute pulmonary oedema.
entries.cautions: Respiratory depression is the lethal one; constipation near-universal (co-prescribe a laxative); accumulates in renal impairment via its active metabolite. Additive with benzodiazepines and alcohol.

entries.mechanism: Mu-agonist; well absorbed orally, no troublesome renally-cleared active metabolite.
entries.uses: Severe pain, often preferred over morphine in renal impairment.
entries.cautions: As morphine; substantial misuse and dependence potential.

entries.mechanism: Mu-agonist requiring CYP2D6 activation to hydromorphone.
entries.uses: Moderate-to-severe pain (predominantly US practice).
entries.cautions: Paracetamol ceiling limits dose escalation; major driver of the US opioid epidemic.

entries.mechanism: Potent mu-agonist, roughly five times morphine by weight.
entries.uses: Severe pain; useful where morphine is poorly tolerated.
entries.cautions: Potency errors on conversion are a recognised cause of fatal overdose.

entries.mechanism: Rapidly converted to morphine; high lipid solubility gives fast CNS entry and small-volume injection.
entries.uses: Severe pain and palliative care (UK); acute pulmonary oedema.
entries.cautions: As morphine but faster onset; high dependence liability. Controlled drug.

entries.mechanism: Very potent, highly lipophilic mu-agonist — the lipophilicity is what lets it cross skin and the blood-brain barrier.
entries.uses: Anaesthesia; transdermal patches for stable chronic and cancer pain.
entries.cautions: Extreme potency means a tiny margin between dose and lethal dose — illicit versions are a leading cause of overdose death. Patches take hours to work and hours to wear off; heat increases absorption.

entries.mechanism: Potent mu-agonists; remifentanil is cleared by plasma esterases, giving offset independent of organ function.
entries.uses: Intraoperative analgesia and total intravenous anaesthesia.
entries.cautions: Profound respiratory depression; chest-wall rigidity; no analgesia persists after stopping remifentanil.

entries.mechanism: Mu-agonist with NMDA antagonism; very long and variable half-life.
entries.uses: Opioid substitution therapy; cancer pain.
entries.cautions: QT prolongation; accumulation over days risks delayed fatal respiratory depression during titration.

entries.mechanism: High receptor affinity but submaximal efficacy — a ceiling on respiratory depression, and it displaces full agonists.
entries.uses: Opioid substitution; transdermal patches for chronic pain.
entries.cautions: Precipitates withdrawal if given soon after a full agonist; naloxone reverses it poorly because of tight binding.

entries.mechanism: Mu-agonist with antimuscarinic activity; metabolite norpethidine is neurotoxic.
entries.uses: Historically labour and biliary colic; now largely superseded.
entries.cautions: Norpethidine accumulation causes seizures; severe interaction with MAOIs.

entries.mechanism: Mu-agonist on the gut myenteric plexus; P-glycoprotein pumps it out of the CNS so it does not reach the brain.
entries.uses: Symptomatic control of diarrhoea.
entries.cautions: Avoid in colitis or suspected infective diarrhoea (toxic megacolon); massive misuse doses cause fatal QT arrhythmias.

entries.mechanism: Binds mu receptors with high affinity but zero efficacy, physically displacing the opioid — the textbook clinical use of competitive antagonism.
entries.uses: Emergency reversal of opioid overdose (IV, IM or intranasal).
entries.cautions: Short half-life — the opioid may outlast it and the patient re-sedate; precipitates acute withdrawal in dependent users.

entries.mechanism: Sustained mu blockade orally or by depot injection.
entries.uses: Relapse prevention in opioid and alcohol dependence.
entries.cautions: Precipitates withdrawal; renders opioid analgesia ineffective; hepatotoxicity at high dose.

entries.mechanism: Block gut opioid receptors without crossing into the brain, relieving constipation without losing analgesia.
entries.uses: Opioid-induced constipation resistant to laxatives.
entries.cautions: Abdominal pain; avoid in bowel obstruction.

entries.mechanism: Binds tubulin and disrupts the microtubules inflammatory cells use to migrate to urate crystals.
entries.uses: Acute gout flare; prophylaxis when starting urate-lowering therapy; pericarditis.
entries.cautions: Dose-limiting diarrhoea; marrow suppression and neuromyopathy in overdose or renal impairment; narrow margin.

entries.mechanism: Blocks the enzyme that makes uric acid, lowering the body's urate load over months.
entries.uses: Long-term prevention of gout; tumour lysis prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: Never start during an acute attack — shifting urate worsens it. Rash and rare severe hypersensitivity (HLA- B*58:01); interacts dangerously with azathioprine.

entries.mechanism: As allopurinol, by a different chemical route.
entries.uses: Gout prevention where allopurinol is unsuitable.
entries.cautions: Cardiovascular mortality signal in established heart disease.

entries.mechanism: Block renal tubular reabsorption of urate, increasing excretion.
entries.uses: Gout prevention in under-excretors.
entries.cautions: Avoid in urate stones or renal impairment; maintain fluid intake.

entries.mechanism: Enzymatically converts urate to soluble allantoin — supplying an enzyme humans lost in evolution.
entries.uses: Tumour lysis syndrome with severe hyperuricaemia.
entries.cautions: Haemolysis in G6PD deficiency; anaphylaxis.

entries.mechanism: As rasburicase, formulated for repeated dosing.
entries.uses: Refractory tophaceous gout.
entries.cautions: Infusion reactions; anti-drug antibodies; contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.

entries.mechanism: Constricts dilated cranial vessels and dampens trigeminal nociceptive transmission.
entries.uses: Acute migraine; cluster headache (subcutaneous).
entries.cautions: Contraindicated in significant cardiovascular disease precisely because it constricts vessels; chest tightness; medication-overuse headache.

entries.mechanism: As sumatriptan, differing in onset and duration.
entries.uses: Acute migraine.
entries.cautions: Same vascular cautions; serotonergic load with SSRIs.

entries.mechanism: Small-molecule blockade of the calcitonin gene-related peptide receptor.
entries.uses: Acute and preventive migraine treatment.
entries.cautions: No vasoconstriction, so usable where triptans are contraindicated; hepatic interactions via CYP3A4.

entries.mechanism: Block CGRP or its receptor — the neuropeptide driving migraine.
entries.uses: Prevention of frequent or chronic migraine.
entries.cautions: Injection-site reactions, constipation; a genuinely new mechanism rather than a borrowed one.

entries.mechanism: Reduces migraine frequency by mechanisms still debated.
entries.uses: Migraine prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: Avoid in asthma; fatigue and cold extremities.

entries.mechanism: Sodium-channel blockade, GABA enhancement, glutamate antagonism, carbonic anhydrase inhibition.
entries.uses: Migraine prevention; epilepsy.
entries.cautions: Weight loss, paraesthesia, word-finding difficulty, renal stones; teratogenic.

entries.mechanism: Prophylactic agents acting on vascular and serotonergic pathways.
entries.uses: Migraine prophylaxis where beta-blockers unsuitable.
entries.cautions: Weight gain, sedation; flunarizine causes parkinsonism and depression.

entries.mechanism: Positive modulation of GABA-A. Lipophilicity gives near-instant onset; redistribution out of the brain gives the equally rapid offset.
entries.uses: Induction and maintenance of anaesthesia; ICU sedation; procedural sedation.
entries.cautions: Dose-dependent apnoea and hypotension; pain on injection; propofol infusion syndrome with prolonged high-dose use.

entries.mechanism: Enhances GABA-A and at high concentration opens the chloride channel directly — unlike benzodiazepines, so there is no ceiling and overdose is lethal.
entries.uses: Rapid sequence induction; status epilepticus; raised intracranial pressure.
entries.cautions: Profound cardiovascular depression; tissue necrosis on extravasation; precipitates acute porphyria.

entries.mechanism: Blocks NMDA receptors producing dissociative anaesthesia with preserved airway reflexes and cardiovascular stimulation.
entries.uses: Anaesthesia in haemodynamic instability and pre-hospital care; analgesia; treatment-resistant depression (esketamine).
entries.cautions: Emergence delirium and hallucinations; raised secretions; misuse potential and bladder toxicity with chronic use.

entries.mechanism: GABA-A modulation with minimal cardiovascular effect.
entries.uses: Induction in haemodynamic compromise.
entries.cautions: Suppresses adrenal steroidogenesis after even a single dose; myoclonus.

entries.mechanism: Enhance inhibitory and depress excitatory neurotransmission; excreted largely unchanged by the lungs, so offset depends on ventilation.
entries.uses: Maintenance of general anaesthesia.
entries.cautions: Malignant hyperthermia in susceptible individuals — antidote dantrolene; significant greenhouse impact (desflurane worst).

entries.mechanism: NMDA antagonism with weak anaesthetic potency; rapid on and off.
entries.uses: Labour analgesia, procedural analgesia (Entonox).
entries.cautions: Inactivates vitamin B12 with repeated exposure — megaloblastic anaemia and subacute combined degeneration; expands air-filled spaces.

entries.mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels on nerve axons, preventing impulse propagation from a region while the patient stays awake.
entries.uses: Infiltration, nerve blocks, topical; ventricular arrhythmia (IV).
entries.cautions: Perioral tingling, tinnitus, seizures then cardiac arrest as levels rise. Adrenaline is often added to prolong the block — avoid in end-arterial territories.

entries.mechanism: As lidocaine, with slower onset and much longer duration.
entries.uses: Epidural and spinal anaesthesia; prolonged nerve blocks.
entries.cautions: Bupivacaine is markedly cardiotoxic and its arrest is hard to reverse. Antidote: intravenous lipid emulsion.

entries.mechanism: Sodium-channel blockade; metabolite o-toluidine oxidises haemoglobin.
entries.uses: Dental and IV regional anaesthesia; topical EMLA with lidocaine.
entries.cautions: Methaemoglobinaemia — treated with methylthioninium chloride.

entries.mechanism: Sodium-channel blockade applied to cornea or mucosa.
entries.uses: Ophthalmic examination and minor eye procedures.
entries.cautions: Corneal toxicity and delayed healing with repeated use — never dispensed for home use.

entries.class: Ester local anaesthetic and monoamine reuptake inhibitor
entries.mechanism: Sodium-channel blockade plus vasoconstriction from noradrenaline reuptake inhibition — uniquely both in one molecule.
entries.uses: ENT surgery where a bloodless field is needed.
entries.cautions: Systemic absorption causes arrhythmia and hypertension; controlled drug.

entries.mechanism: Persistently activates the nicotinic receptor at the motor end plate, causing fasciculation then flaccid paralysis; broken down by plasma cholinesterase.
entries.uses: Rapid sequence induction where fast onset and offset matter.
entries.cautions: Hyperkalaemia (dangerous in burns, crush injury, denervation), malignant hyperthermia, muscle pains, prolonged block in cholinesterase deficiency.

entries.mechanism: Competitively antagonises acetylcholine at the nicotinic receptor; fast onset.
entries.uses: Intubation and surgical relaxation.
entries.cautions: Reversed specifically by sugammadex, which encapsulates the molecule.

entries.mechanism: Competitive nicotinic antagonism; degrade spontaneously by Hofmann elimination, independent of liver and kidney.
entries.uses: Muscle relaxation in organ failure and ICU.
entries.cautions: Histamine release with atracurium; laudanosine accumulation in prolonged use.

entries.mechanism: Competitive nicotinic antagonism; renally and hepatically cleared.
entries.uses: Surgical relaxation; ICU ventilation.
entries.cautions: Prolonged block in organ failure; pancuronium causes tachycardia.

entries.mechanism: Raises acetylcholine at the junction, out-competing the blocker. Quaternary — stays out of the CNS.
entries.uses: Reversal of non-depolarising blockade; myasthenia gravis.
entries.cautions: Must be given with an antimuscarinic (glycopyrronium or atropine) or bradycardia and secretions follow.

entries.mechanism: A modified cyclodextrin that encapsulates rocuronium or vecuronium in plasma — it does not touch the receptor at all, it removes the drug.
entries.uses: Rapid reversal of aminosteroid blockade, including deep block.
entries.cautions: Binds progestogens, so contraceptive efficacy is lost for several days — patients must be told.

entries.mechanism: Blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, acting on muscle directly rather than through nerves.
entries.uses: Malignant hyperthermia; neuroleptic malignant syndrome; chronic spasticity.
entries.cautions: Hepatotoxicity with chronic oral use; profound weakness.

entries.mechanism: Blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, so unopposed sympathetic effects dominate — heart rate rises, secretions dry, pupils dilate, gut slows.
entries.uses: Symptomatic bradycardia; drying secretions; organophosphate poisoning; mydriasis.
entries.cautions: “Can't see, can't pee, can't spit, can't shit”, plus tachycardia and confusion. Caution in glaucoma and prostatic enlargement.

entries.mechanism: Blocks M receptors on smooth muscle; quaternary, so no CNS entry.
entries.uses: Abdominal and biliary colic, IBS cramps; secretions in palliative care.
entries.cautions: Antimuscarinic effects; avoid in paralytic ileus and glaucoma.

entries.mechanism: Blocks muscarinic receptors in vestibular and vomiting pathways and on secretory glands.
entries.uses: Motion sickness (patch); drying secretions in palliative care.
entries.cautions: Sedation, confusion in the elderly, dry mouth, blurred vision.

entries.mechanism: Direct smooth-muscle relaxation plus muscarinic blockade in the gut.
entries.uses: Irritable bowel syndrome with cramping.
entries.cautions: Anticholinergic burden; avoid in the elderly and in infants.

entries.mechanism: Relax intestinal smooth muscle without muscarinic blockade, so no anticholinergic effects.
entries.uses: Irritable bowel syndrome.
entries.cautions: Well tolerated; peppermint oil causes heartburn.

entries.mechanism: Blocks airway M3 receptors, delivered locally to minimise systemic effect.
entries.uses: COPD; add-on in acute asthma.
entries.cautions: Dry mouth; paradoxical bronchospasm; glaucoma if nebulised into the eyes.

entries.mechanism: Prolonged M3 blockade — essentially atropine for the lungs, once daily.
entries.uses: Maintenance in COPD and severe asthma.
entries.cautions: Dry mouth; urinary retention in susceptible men.

entries.mechanism: Blocks M3 in the detrusor, relaxing an overactive bladder.
entries.uses: Overactive bladder, urge incontinence.
entries.cautions: Predictably anticholinergic — dry mouth, constipation, confusion; poor choice in the frail elderly.

entries.mechanism: More selective M3 antagonism than oxybutynin.
entries.uses: Overactive bladder.
entries.cautions: Better tolerated but same class effects; QT caution with solifenacin.

entries.mechanism: Peripheral muscarinic blockade with no CNS penetration.
entries.uses: Drying secretions; reversal of neostigmine's muscarinic effects; hyperhidrosis.
entries.cautions: Tachycardia, dry mouth.

entries.class: Antihistamine with antiserotonergic and antimuscarinic action
entries.mechanism: Blocks H1 and 5-HT2 receptors; appetite stimulation follows from the serotonergic block.
entries.uses: Appetite stimulation; serotonin syndrome; cold urticaria.
entries.cautions: Marked sedation; anticholinergic burden.

entries.mechanism: Mimics acetylcholine — constricts the pupil, increases aqueous drainage, stimulates saliva. The deliberate mirror image of atropine.
entries.uses: Glaucoma; dry mouth in Sjögren's and post-radiotherapy.
entries.cautions: Brow ache, blurred near vision, sweating.

entries.mechanism: Stimulates bladder and gut smooth muscle.
entries.uses: Urinary retention without obstruction.
entries.cautions: Cramps, bradycardia, bronchospasm.

entries.mechanism: Prevents acetylcholine breakdown, raising its concentration at the neuromuscular junction; quaternary, so peripheral only.
entries.uses: Maintenance treatment of myasthenia gravis.
entries.cautions: Cramps, diarrhoea, salivation; distinguishing cholinergic from myasthenic crisis is the clinical challenge.

entries.mechanism: Regenerates acetylcholinesterase before the enzyme-organophosphate bond “ages” irreversibly.
entries.uses: Organophosphate poisoning, alongside atropine.
entries.cautions: Must be given early; ineffective once ageing has occurred.

entries.mechanism: Activates alpha-1 (vasoconstriction), beta-1 (cardiac stimulation) and beta-2 (bronchodilation) simultaneously — one drug, three receptors, three problems solved.
entries.uses: Anaphylaxis (first-line IM into the thigh); cardiac arrest; added to local anaesthetics; croup (nebulised).
entries.cautions: Palpitations, tremor, anxiety, hypertension if the wrong route or dose is used. IM is far safer than IV in anaphylaxis.

entries.mechanism: Potent vasoconstriction raising systemic vascular resistance with modest beta-1 effect.
entries.uses: Septic and vasodilatory shock (central line, ICU).
entries.cautions: Tissue necrosis on extravasation; reflex bradycardia; organ ischaemia if overdone.

entries.mechanism: Increases myocardial contractility and output with mild vasodilation.
entries.uses: Cardiogenic shock, low-output states; stress echocardiography.
entries.cautions: Tachyarrhythmias, increased myocardial oxygen demand.

entries.mechanism: Dopaminergic at low dose, beta-1 at moderate, alpha-1 at high dose.
entries.uses: Shock (largely superseded by noradrenaline).
entries.cautions: Arrhythmias; the historical “renal dose” concept is discredited.

entries.mechanism: Pure vasoconstriction; also a mydriatic without cycloplegia.
entries.uses: Hypotension under anaesthesia; pupil dilation; topical decongestion.
entries.cautions: Reflex bradycardia. Orally it is destroyed by first-pass metabolism, so oral phenylephrine is a poor decongestant — a bioavailability problem, not a receptor one.

entries.mechanism: Acts directly on alpha-1 and indirectly by displacing noradrenaline from vesicles. Survives first-pass metabolism, which is why it works by mouth — and reaches the whole circulation, which is where its problems come from.
entries.uses: Nasal and sinus congestion.
entries.cautions: Hypertension, tachycardia, insomnia; avoid in ischaemic heart disease and hyperthyroidism; urinary retention in prostatism. Hypertensive crisis with MAOIs. Sale restricted as a methamphetamine precursor. No rebound congestion, unlike topical agents.

entries.mechanism: Direct alpha and beta agonism plus indirect noradrenaline release; enters the CNS more readily than pseudoephedrine.
entries.uses: Hypotension during spinal anaesthesia, particularly in obstetrics.
entries.cautions: Tachyphylaxis develops rapidly as vesicular noradrenaline depletes — the signature of an indirect agent. Tachycardia, anxiety.

entries.mechanism: Prodrug producing sustained peripheral vasoconstriction.
entries.uses: Severe orthostatic hypotension.
entries.cautions: Supine hypertension, scalp tingling.

entries.mechanism: Stimulates presynaptic alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem, reducing sympathetic outflow — an agonist that lowers blood pressure.
entries.uses: Resistant hypertension; ADHD; menopausal flushing; opioid withdrawal.
entries.cautions: Sedation, dry mouth, and dangerous rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal.

entries.mechanism: Central alpha-2 stimulation producing sedation without significant respiratory depression.
entries.uses: ICU and procedural sedation.
entries.cautions: Bradycardia and hypotension.

entries.mechanism: Relaxes the detrusor during filling by a sympathetic route, avoiding muscarinic blockade entirely.
entries.uses: Overactive bladder, especially where anticholinergic burden is a concern.
entries.cautions: Hypertension; raises metoprolol and digoxin levels.

entries.mechanism: Blocks alpha-1 on vessels giving vasodilation, and relaxes prostate and bladder-neck smooth muscle.
entries.uses: Resistant hypertension; benign prostatic enlargement.
entries.cautions: Postural hypotension, especially the first-dose phenomenon — hence night-time initiation.

entries.mechanism: Selective for prostatic alpha-1A subtype, so urinary benefit with less blood-pressure effect.
entries.uses: Benign prostatic hyperplasia; medical expulsive therapy for ureteric stones.
entries.cautions: Retrograde ejaculation; intraoperative floppy iris syndrome — tell the ophthalmologist before cataract surgery.

entries.mechanism: Alpha-1 blockade with CNS penetration.
entries.uses: PTSD-related nightmares; hypertension; Raynaud's.
entries.cautions: Marked first-dose hypotension; short half-life needs multiple daily doses.

entries.mechanism: Irreversible (phenoxybenzamine) or reversible alpha-1 and alpha-2 blockade.
entries.uses: Pre-operative preparation in phaeochromocytoma — always before beta-blockade.
entries.cautions: Profound hypotension and reflex tachycardia; beta-blockade first risks unopposed alpha crisis.

entries.mechanism: Blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme so less angiotensin II is made — vasodilation plus less aldosterone; also protects the diabetic kidney and unloads a failing heart.
entries.uses: Hypertension, heart failure, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy.
entries.cautions: Dry cough (bradykinin accumulation); hyperkalaemia; first-dose hypotension; falling eGFR; contraindicated in pregnancy; rare angioedema.

entries.mechanism: As ramipril; already active, no hepatic conversion needed.
entries.uses: Hypertension, heart failure, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy.
entries.cautions: Same class profile; monitor U&Es after initiation and dose change.

entries.mechanism: As ramipril; enalapril and perindopril are prodrugs, captopril is short-acting and already active.
entries.uses: Hypertension, heart failure, nephropathy.
entries.cautions: Same class profile; captopril causes taste disturbance and rash.

entries.mechanism: Blocks the angiotensin-II receptor directly — the same end result as an ACE inhibitor but without the cough, because bradykinin is untouched.
entries.uses: Hypertension, heart failure, diabetic nephropathy; the go-to when ACEi cough is intolerable.
entries.cautions: Hyperkalaemia; avoid in pregnancy; otherwise well tolerated.

entries.mechanism: As losartan, with differing potency and duration.
entries.uses: Hypertension, heart failure, nephropathy.
entries.cautions: Same class profile; olmesartan rarely causes a sprue-like enteropathy.

entries.mechanism: Sacubitril blocks neprilysin, preserving beneficial natriuretic peptides, while valsartan blocks AT1 — two arms at once.
entries.uses: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, replacing an ACEi/ARB.
entries.cautions: Must not overlap with an ACE inhibitor — 36-hour washout to avoid angioedema. Hypotension, hyperkalaemia.

entries.mechanism: Blocks aldosterone in the distal nephron, and improves survival in heart failure through effects beyond fluid loss.
entries.uses: Heart failure, resistant hypertension, ascites, primary hyperaldosteronism, acne and hirsutism.
entries.cautions: Hyperkalaemia (dangerous stacked with ACEi/ARB and NSAIDs); gynaecomastia from off-target sex-hormone receptor binding.

entries.mechanism: As spironolactone without sex-hormone receptor affinity.
entries.uses: Post-MI heart failure; where gynaecomastia is unacceptable.
entries.cautions: Hyperkalaemia; more expensive.

entries.mechanism: Blocks renin itself, at the top of the cascade.
entries.uses: Hypertension (rarely used).
entries.cautions: Never combine with ACEi/ARB — renal harm and hyperkalaemia.

entries.mechanism: Blocks L-type calcium entry into vascular smooth muscle, so arteries relax and blood pressure falls.
entries.uses: Hypertension, stable angina.
entries.cautions: Ankle swelling, flushing, headache, palpitations — all predictable from vasodilation, nuisances rather than heart failure.

entries.mechanism: As amlodipine; modified-release used in pregnancy.
entries.uses: Hypertension in pregnancy, angina, Raynaud's, tocolysis.
entries.cautions: Immediate-release causes reflex tachycardia and is avoided in hypertension.

entries.mechanism: As amlodipine.
entries.uses: Hypertension, angina.
entries.cautions: Same vasodilatory effects; lercanidipine causes less ankle oedema.

entries.mechanism: Blocks cardiac calcium channels more than vascular — slows rate and AV conduction and reduces contractility.
entries.uses: Rate control in AF, SVT, angina, cluster headache prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: Never combine with a beta-blocker — dangerous bradycardia or complete heart block. Marked constipation. Avoid in heart failure.

entries.mechanism: Intermediate between verapamil and the dihydropyridines in cardiac versus vascular action.
entries.uses: Angina, rate control, hypertension.
entries.cautions: Bradycardia and heart block, especially with beta-blockers; CYP3A4 inhibitor.

entries.mechanism: Blocks the Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule; a longer-term vasodilator effect adds to the benefit.
entries.uses: Hypertension; oedema; paradoxically reduces urine output in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
entries.cautions: Hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, raised glucose, raised urate (gout) and raised calcium — thiazides push several things the wrong way at once. Photosensitivity; skin cancer signal.

entries.mechanism: As hydrochlorothiazide; the traditional UK and Commonwealth agent.
entries.uses: Hypertension, especially in older patients.
entries.cautions: Same metabolic profile.

entries.mechanism: As thiazides, with a relatively greater vasodilator component.
entries.uses: Hypertension; often preferred first-line.
entries.cautions: Same metabolic profile; QT prolongation with hypokalaemia.

entries.mechanism: Longer acting and more potent than hydrochlorothiazide at equivalent doses.
entries.uses: Hypertension, with the strongest outcome evidence of the class.
entries.cautions: More marked hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia.

entries.mechanism: Blocks the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb — the most powerful diuretic site, hence its use in emergencies.
entries.uses: Fluid overload in heart failure, pulmonary oedema, renal and hepatic oedema.
entries.cautions: Dehydration, hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, renal impairment, ototoxicity at high IV doses, raised urate.

entries.mechanism: As furosemide; more reliable oral absorption in gut oedema.
entries.uses: Heart failure where furosemide absorption is poor.
entries.cautions: As furosemide; torasemide has a longer duration.

entries.mechanism: Block the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the collecting duct.
entries.uses: Adjunct to thiazides or loops to conserve potassium; Liddle syndrome.
entries.cautions: Hyperkalaemia, particularly with ACEi/ARB; triamterene causes renal stones.

entries.mechanism: Reduces bicarbonate reabsorption proximally and aqueous humour production in the eye.
entries.uses: Glaucoma, altitude sickness, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, some epilepsies.
entries.cautions: Metabolic acidosis, paraesthesia, renal stones; sulfonamide reactions.

entries.mechanism: Filtered but not reabsorbed, drawing water osmotically into tubular fluid and out of the brain.
entries.uses: Raised intracranial pressure; cerebral oedema.
entries.cautions: Volume overload before diuresis; electrolyte disturbance.

entries.mechanism: Blocks ADH at the collecting duct producing free-water loss without sodium loss (aquaresis).
entries.uses: Hyponatraemia from SIADH; autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
entries.cautions: Over-rapid sodium correction risks osmotic demyelination; hepatotoxicity.

entries.mechanism: Blocks cardiac beta-1 receptors giving a slower rate, weaker contraction, lower blood pressure and reduced myocardial oxygen demand.
entries.uses: Heart failure (start low, titrate slowly), hypertension, angina, post-MI, rate control.
entries.cautions: Fatigue, cold hands, bradycardia, vivid dreams; masks hypoglycaemia warning; caution in asthma; never stop abruptly.

entries.mechanism: As bisoprolol; the succinate modified-release form is the heart-failure agent.
entries.uses: Heart failure, angina, arrhythmia, migraine prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: CYP2D6 substrate; standard beta-blocker cautions.

entries.mechanism: As bisoprolol; renally cleared and hydrophilic, so fewer CNS effects.
entries.uses: Hypertension, angina, rate control.
entries.cautions: Accumulates in renal impairment; not first-line in uncomplicated hypertension over 60.

entries.mechanism: Non-selective beta blockade plus vasodilating alpha-1 antagonism.
entries.uses: Heart failure, hypertension, portal hypertension.
entries.cautions: Postural hypotension; standard beta-blocker cautions.

entries.mechanism: Blocks beta-1 and beta-2; lipophilic, so it crosses into the brain.
entries.uses: Tremor, physical symptoms of anxiety, migraine prophylaxis, thyrotoxicosis, portal hypertension, infantile haemangioma.
entries.cautions: Beta-2 blockade causes bronchospasm — avoid in asthma. Vivid dreams from CNS entry.

entries.mechanism: Mixed blockade lowering BP without reflex tachycardia.
entries.uses: Hypertension in pregnancy and pre-eclampsia; hypertensive emergencies.
entries.cautions: Hepatotoxicity (rare); scalp tingling.

entries.mechanism: Beta blockade plus potassium-channel blockade prolonging repolarisation.
entries.uses: Maintenance of sinus rhythm in atrial fibrillation.
entries.cautions: QT prolongation and torsades — ECG monitoring on initiation.

entries.mechanism: Highly beta-1 selective, additionally releasing nitric oxide from endothelium.
entries.uses: Hypertension; heart failure in the elderly.
entries.cautions: Fewer metabolic effects than other beta-blockers.

entries.mechanism: Hydrolysed by red-cell esterases, half-life about nine minutes.
entries.uses: Perioperative tachycardia; titratable rate control.
entries.cautions: Effect wears off within minutes of stopping — which is the point.

entries.mechanism: Releases NO, raising cGMP in vascular smooth muscle — predominantly venodilation, reducing preload and cardiac work.
entries.uses: Acute angina (sublingual); acute heart failure and ACS (infusion); anal fissure (topical).
entries.cautions: Headache, flushing, postural hypotension; tolerance with continuous exposure. Catastrophic hypotension with PDE5 inhibitors.

entries.mechanism: As GTN with sustained levels; mononitrate has no first-pass loss.
entries.uses: Angina prophylaxis; heart failure with hydralazine.
entries.cautions: Asymmetric dosing preserves a nitrate-free period to avoid tolerance.

entries.mechanism: Selectively inhibits the sinoatrial pacemaker current, slowing rate without affecting contractility or blood pressure.
entries.uses: Heart failure and angina where beta-blockers are insufficient or not tolerated.
entries.cautions: Luminous visual phenomena (phosphenes) — the same channel family exists in the retina; only works in sinus rhythm.

entries.mechanism: Opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels (arterial dilation) with a nitrate moiety (venodilation).
entries.uses: Refractory angina.
entries.cautions: Painful mucosal, anal and gastrointestinal ulceration — distinctive and often missed.

entries.mechanism: Reduces the late inward sodium current, lowering calcium overload and wall tension.
entries.uses: Chronic angina as add-on.
entries.cautions: QT prolongation; constipation, dizziness.

entries.mechanism: Inhibits the cardiac Na/K-ATPase, raising intracellular sodium and hence calcium (more forceful contraction), and slows AV conduction via vagal tone.
entries.uses: Rate control in atrial fibrillation; symptom control in heart failure.
entries.cautions: Narrow therapeutic index — nausea, yellow-green haloes, confusion, arrhythmia. Hypokalaemia worsens toxicity (they compete at the same pump). Antidote: digoxin-specific antibody.

entries.mechanism: Block PDE3, raising cardiac cAMP independently of the beta receptor — so they work even in beta-blocked or downregulated hearts.
entries.uses: Acute decompensated heart failure; post-cardiac-surgery low output.
entries.cautions: Hypotension from vasodilation; arrhythmias; increased mortality with chronic oral use.

entries.mechanism: Increases troponin C sensitivity to calcium, improving contraction without raising intracellular calcium or oxygen demand.
entries.uses: Acute decompensated heart failure.
entries.cautions: Hypotension; long-acting metabolite prolongs effect for days.

entries.mechanism: Directly stimulates sGC, restoring NO-cGMP signalling impaired in heart failure.
entries.uses: Worsening chronic HFrEF after a decompensation.
entries.cautions: Hypotension, anaemia; contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors and nitrates.

entries.mechanism: Reduces excessive actin-myosin cross-bridge formation, lessening hypercontractility and outflow obstruction — the first drug to target the sarcomere itself.
entries.uses: Symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
entries.cautions: Systolic dysfunction requiring echo monitoring; CYP2C19 dependent.

entries.mechanism: Relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle by an incompletely defined mechanism, reducing afterload.
entries.uses: Hypertensive emergencies in pregnancy; heart failure with isosorbide dinitrate.
entries.cautions: Reflex tachycardia and fluid retention; drug-induced lupus in slow acetylators.

entries.mechanism: Converted to a false transmitter that stimulates brainstem alpha-2 receptors, reducing sympathetic outflow.
entries.uses: Hypertension in pregnancy — the longest safety record in this setting.
entries.cautions: Sedation, depression; positive direct Coombs test and haemolytic anaemia; drug-induced hepatitis.

entries.mechanism: Opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels in arterial smooth muscle, causing powerful vasodilation.
entries.uses: Severe resistant hypertension; topically for androgenetic alopecia.
entries.cautions: Marked fluid retention and reflex tachycardia; hypertrichosis — which is why the topical form exists.

entries.mechanism: Releases NO directly, dilating arteries and veins with onset and offset in seconds.
entries.uses: Hypertensive emergency needing minute-to-minute control.
entries.cautions: Cyanide and thiocyanate accumulation with prolonged infusion; light-sensitive.

entries.mechanism: Blocks sodium channels and prolongs repolarisation; also antimuscarinic.
entries.uses: Brugada syndrome; historically atrial fibrillation; severe malaria (as quinine's isomer relative).
entries.cautions: QT prolongation and torsades; cinchonism (tinnitus, deafness, visual blurring); thrombocytopenia.

entries.mechanism: Sodium-channel blockade with active metabolite prolonging repolarisation.
entries.uses: Wide-complex tachycardia; pre-excited atrial fibrillation.
entries.cautions: Drug-induced lupus with prolonged use; QT prolongation; agranulocytosis.

entries.mechanism: Sodium-channel blockade with marked negative inotropy and antimuscarinic action.
entries.uses: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (the negative inotropy is the point); vasovagal syncope.
entries.cautions: Urinary retention, dry mouth, heart failure.

entries.mechanism: Preferentially blocks sodium channels in ischaemic, rapidly firing myocardium.
entries.uses: Ventricular arrhythmias, particularly peri-infarct.
entries.cautions: CNS toxicity — perioral tingling, confusion, seizures; extensive first-pass metabolism so not oral.

entries.mechanism: Oral lidocaine analogue with the same use-dependent sodium blockade.
entries.uses: Ventricular arrhythmia; myotonia in myotonic dystrophy.
entries.cautions: Nausea, tremor, ataxia; narrow margin.

entries.mechanism: Markedly slows the phase-0 upstroke, depressing conduction.
entries.uses: Cardioversion and maintenance of sinus rhythm in AF; “pill in the pocket”.
entries.cautions: Strictly avoided in structural or ischaemic heart disease — proarrhythmic mortality (the CAST trial lesson).

entries.mechanism: Prolongs repolarisation by blocking potassium channels, with additional sodium, calcium and beta-blocking actions.
entries.uses: Atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, including in structural heart disease; cardiac arrest.
entries.cautions: Enormous volume of distribution and a half-life of weeks. Thyroid dysfunction both ways (from its iodine), pulmonary fibrosis, hepatitis, corneal deposits, grey-blue skin, photosensitivity. Raises digoxin and warfarin levels.

entries.mechanism: Amiodarone analogue without iodine.
entries.uses: Paroxysmal AF without heart failure.
entries.cautions: Contraindicated in heart failure and permanent AF — increased mortality; hepatotoxicity.

entries.mechanism: Transiently blocks AV nodal conduction via A1 receptors; half-life of seconds.
entries.uses: Termination or diagnosis of supraventricular tachycardia (rapid IV bolus).
entries.cautions: A brief, alarming sense of impending doom, flushing and chest tightness — warn the patient. Avoid in asthma; antagonised by caffeine and theophylline.

entries.mechanism: Stabilises the myocardial membrane and shortens the QT.
entries.uses: Torsades de pointes; eclampsia; severe asthma.
entries.cautions: Loss of deep tendon reflexes signals toxicity. Antidote: calcium gluconate.

entries.mechanism: Blocks the rate-limiting enzyme of hepatic cholesterol synthesis; the liver compensates by upregulating LDL receptors and pulling LDL out of the blood — that compensation is where most of the benefit comes from.
entries.uses: Primary and secondary cardiovascular prevention; hypercholesterolaemia.
entries.cautions: Myalgia and rarely rhabdomyolysis; deranged LFTs. Long half-life so timing is flexible.

entries.mechanism: As atorvastatin; short-acting.
entries.uses: As atorvastatin.
entries.cautions: Taken at night because cholesterol synthesis peaks overnight. CYP3A4 substrate — grapefruit juice and clarithromycin raise levels and muscle risk.

entries.mechanism: As above; pravastatin is not CYP3A4-dependent, reducing interactions.
entries.uses: As above, including in patients on interacting drugs.
entries.cautions: Same class profile; rosuvastatin is the most potent.

entries.mechanism: Blocks the NPC1L1 sterol transporter in the intestinal brush border, reducing dietary and biliary cholesterol absorption.
entries.uses: Add-on when a statin alone is insufficient or not tolerated.
entries.cautions: Generally well tolerated; myalgia when combined with a statin.

entries.mechanism: Prevent PCSK9 from destroying hepatic LDL receptors, so more receptors survive to clear LDL.
entries.uses: Familial hypercholesterolaemia; very high-risk patients not at target.
entries.cautions: Injection-site reactions; cost restricts use.

entries.mechanism: Silences hepatic PCSK9 messenger RNA, giving sustained LDL reduction from twice-yearly injection.
entries.uses: As PCSK9 antibodies, with far less frequent dosing.
entries.cautions: Injection-site reactions.

entries.mechanism: Blocks cholesterol synthesis upstream of HMG-CoA reductase; activated only in liver, not muscle, which is why it spares myalgia.
entries.uses: Hypercholesterolaemia in statin intolerance.
entries.cautions: Raises uric acid and precipitates gout; tendon rupture.

entries.mechanism: Activate PPAR-alpha, increasing lipoprotein lipase activity and lowering triglycerides.
entries.uses: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia; mixed dyslipidaemia.
entries.cautions: Myopathy risk compounded with statins (worst with gemfibrozil); gallstones; raised creatinine.

entries.drug: Omega-3 acid ethyl esters / icosapent ethyl
entries.mechanism: Lower hepatic triglyceride synthesis; icosapent ethyl additionally stabilises plaque.
entries.uses: Hypertriglyceridaemia; residual risk on a statin.
entries.cautions: Atrial fibrillation; bleeding tendency; fishy aftertaste.

entries.mechanism: Bind bile acids in the gut, forcing the liver to consume cholesterol to make more.
entries.uses: Hypercholesterolaemia; bile-acid diarrhoea; pruritus of cholestasis.
entries.cautions: Bloating, constipation; bind other drugs and fat-soluble vitamins — separate dosing.

entries.mechanism: Permanently acetylates platelet COX-1, abolishing thromboxane A2 for the platelet's whole lifespan.
entries.uses: Secondary prevention after MI, stroke and TIA; acute coronary syndromes.
entries.cautions: GI bleeding and dyspepsia; here the “side effect” of reduced clotting is the therapeutic goal.

entries.mechanism: Irreversibly blocks the platelet ADP receptor, preventing GPIIb/ IIIa activation. Requires CYP2C19 activation.
entries.uses: ACS and post-stent (with aspirin); alternative to aspirin in stroke and peripheral arterial disease.
entries.cautions: Bleeding; CYP2C19 poor metabolisers get reduced benefit.

entries.mechanism: Ticagrelor binds reversibly and needs no activation; prasugrel is a more reliably activated prodrug.
entries.uses: Acute coronary syndrome, especially with PCI.
entries.cautions: More bleeding than clopidogrel; ticagrelor causes dyspnoea and bradycardia; prasugrel contraindicated after stroke.

entries.mechanism: Raises platelet cAMP and adenosine levels, inhibiting aggregation and dilating vessels.
entries.uses: Secondary stroke prevention with aspirin; pharmacological stress testing.
entries.cautions: Headache (often limiting), flushing, hypotension.

entries.mechanism: Block the final common pathway of platelet aggregation — fibrinogen cross-linking.
entries.uses: High-risk PCI, intravenous only.
entries.cautions: Major bleeding; thrombocytopenia.

entries.mechanism: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, so factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S) cannot be carboxylated. Existing factors must decay first — hence slow onset and an early procoagulant window.
entries.uses: Mechanical heart valves, atrial fibrillation, VTE where a DOAC is unsuitable, antiphospholipid syndrome.
entries.cautions: Narrow therapeutic index requiring INR monitoring; enormous interaction list (CYP2C9, antibiotics, dietary vitamin K); teratogenic. Antidote: vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate.

entries.mechanism: Binds antithrombin and accelerates its inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa many thousand-fold.
entries.uses: Acute VTE, ACS, bridging where rapid reversal may be needed; preferred in severe renal failure.
entries.cautions: Bleeding; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; osteoporosis with long use. Monitored by APTT. Antidote: protamine.

entries.mechanism: Shorter chains preferentially inactivate factor Xa rather than thrombin, giving predictable kinetics without routine monitoring.
entries.uses: VTE prophylaxis and treatment; ACS; anticoagulation in pregnancy.
entries.cautions: Accumulates in renal impairment; lower HIT risk; only partially reversed by protamine.

entries.mechanism: Pure indirect factor Xa inhibition via antithrombin.
entries.uses: VTE prophylaxis and treatment; option in HIT.
entries.cautions: Renally cleared; no effective reversal agent.

entries.mechanism: Directly and reversibly blocks factor Xa without needing antithrombin.
entries.uses: AF stroke prevention; VTE treatment and prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: No routine monitoring, but adherence matters because the effect fades within a day. Dose-reduce for age, weight and renal function. Antidote: andexanet alfa.

entries.mechanism: As apixaban; rivaroxaban needs food for absorption at treatment doses.
entries.uses: AF, VTE; low-dose rivaroxaban with aspirin in vascular disease.
entries.cautions: Contraindicated in severe renal impairment and antiphospholipid syndrome.

entries.mechanism: Directly inhibits thrombin rather than factor Xa.
entries.uses: AF, VTE.
entries.cautions: Dyspepsia; heavily renally cleared. Antidote: idarucizumab, the first specific DOAC reversal agent.

entries.mechanism: Bind thrombin directly, independent of antithrombin.
entries.uses: Anticoagulation in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; PCI.
entries.cautions: Bleeding; no antidote; argatroban is hepatically cleared.

entries.mechanism: Converts plasminogen to plasmin on the fibrin surface, dissolving formed clot — a clot-buster rather than a clot-preventer.
entries.uses: Acute ischaemic stroke within the window; massive pulmonary embolism; STEMI where PCI is unavailable.
entries.cautions: Intracranial and systemic haemorrhage — an exhaustive contraindication checklist applies.

entries.mechanism: Longer half-life and greater fibrin specificity, so a single bolus suffices.
entries.uses: STEMI; increasingly acute stroke.
entries.cautions: As alteplase.

entries.mechanism: A streptococcal protein that complexes with plasminogen to generate plasmin — not fibrin-specific, so it lyses systemically.
entries.uses: STEMI where newer agents are unaffordable.
entries.cautions: Being foreign protein it causes allergic reactions and hypotension, and antibodies prevent re-use within years — a problem no recombinant agent has.

entries.mechanism: Blocks lysine binding sites on plasminogen, preventing it binding fibrin — the mirror image of alteplase.
entries.uses: Major trauma haemorrhage, post-partum haemorrhage, menorrhagia, surgical bleeding.
entries.cautions: Thrombosis in predisposed patients; seizures at high dose; give early in trauma.

entries.mechanism: Restores gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors.
entries.uses: Warfarin reversal; haemorrhagic disease of the newborn.
entries.cautions: Slow onset (hours); IV route carries a small anaphylactoid risk.

entries.mechanism: Strongly basic peptide that binds and neutralises acidic heparin electrostatically.
entries.uses: Heparin overdose or reversal.
entries.cautions: Hypotension and anaphylaxis; only partially reverses LMWH.

entries.mechanism: Selective antidiuretic action without vasoconstriction; also releases von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from endothelium.
entries.uses: Cranial diabetes insipidus; nocturnal enuresis; mild haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease.
entries.cautions: Hyponatraemia from water retention — fluid restriction and sodium monitoring.

entries.mechanism: Supplies factors II, VII, IX and X immediately, restoring haemostasis far faster than vitamin K.
entries.uses: Major bleeding on warfarin; some coagulopathies.
entries.cautions: Thrombosis; must be given with vitamin K, since factors decay within hours while warfarin persists.

entries.mechanism: FFP supplies all coagulation factors; cryoprecipitate concentrates fibrinogen, factor VIII and von Willebrand factor.
entries.uses: Massive haemorrhage protocols; fibrinogen replacement; DIC.
entries.cautions: Volume overload, transfusion reactions, TRALI; compatibility required.

entries.drug: Red blood cells / platelets / whole blood
entries.mechanism: Restore oxygen-carrying capacity or platelet number directly.
entries.uses: Anaemia with compromise; thrombocytopenic bleeding; massive haemorrhage.
entries.cautions: Transfusion reactions, iron overload with repeated units, TACO and TRALI.

entries.mechanism: Replace the missing clotting factor.
entries.uses: Haemophilia A and B, treatment and prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: Inhibitor (anti-factor antibody) development is the central problem.

entries.mechanism: Bridges factors IXa and X, mimicking factor VIII's job without being factor VIII — so inhibitors do not affect it.
entries.uses: Haemophilia A prophylaxis, including with inhibitors.
entries.cautions: Thrombotic microangiopathy if combined with bypassing agents; standard coagulation assays become misleading.

entries.mechanism: Stimulate megakaryocyte production of platelets.
entries.uses: Chronic immune thrombocytopenia; aplastic anaemia.
entries.cautions: Thrombosis; marrow reticulin; hepatotoxicity with eltrombopag.

entries.mechanism: Supplies iron for haemoglobin synthesis.
entries.uses: Iron-deficiency anaemia.
entries.cautions: Constipation, black stools, nausea; absorption improved by vitamin C, reduced by tea, calcium, PPIs and tetracyclines. Overdose is a paediatric emergency — antidote desferrioxamine.

entries.mechanism: Delivers iron directly, bypassing failed gut absorption.
entries.uses: Iron deficiency with intolerance or malabsorption; CKD; heart failure.
entries.cautions: Anaphylaxis; hypophosphataemia with carboxymaltose; skin staining on extravasation.

entries.mechanism: Substrate for DNA synthesis in erythropoiesis and neural tube closure.
entries.uses: Megaloblastic anaemia; pregnancy prophylaxis; methotrexate cover.
entries.cautions: Never give alone in undiagnosed B12 deficiency — it can precipitate subacute combined degeneration of the cord.

entries.mechanism: Cofactor for methionine synthase and myelin maintenance.
entries.uses: Pernicious anaemia; B12 deficiency; nitrous oxide toxicity.
entries.cautions: Hypokalaemia on rapid correction; hydroxocobalamin is also the cyanide antidote.

entries.mechanism: Stimulate erythroid progenitors in the marrow.
entries.uses: Anaemia of chronic kidney disease; chemotherapy-related anaemia.
entries.cautions: Hypertension, thrombosis; over-correction of haemoglobin increases mortality.

entries.mechanism: Drive neutrophil production and release from the marrow.
entries.uses: Chemotherapy-induced neutropenia; stem-cell mobilisation.
entries.cautions: Bone pain; splenic enlargement.

entries.mechanism: Depletes deoxyribonucleotides; also raises fetal haemoglobin, which is what helps in sickle cell.
entries.uses: Sickle cell disease; chronic myeloid disorders; thrombocythaemia.
entries.cautions: Myelosuppression; leg ulcers; skin changes; teratogenic.

entries.mechanism: Bind excess iron for urinary or faecal excretion.
entries.uses: Transfusional iron overload in thalassaemia and sickle cell; acute iron poisoning.
entries.cautions: Deferasirox: renal and hepatic impairment, GI haemorrhage. Deferiprone: agranulocytosis needing weekly counts.

entries.mechanism: Selectively stimulates airway beta-2 receptors, raising cAMP and relaxing bronchial smooth muscle within minutes.
entries.uses: Acute relief in asthma and COPD; nebulised in acute severe asthma; IV for hyperkalaemia (drives potassium into cells).
entries.cautions: Tremor, tachycardia, palpitations from beta-2 spillover; hypokalaemia and lactic acidosis at high dose. Frequent reliever use signals poor control.

entries.mechanism: As salbutamol; levalbuterol is the active enantiomer.
entries.uses: Asthma; terbutaline for tocolysis.
entries.cautions: As salbutamol.

entries.mechanism: Prolonged beta-2 stimulation; formoterol has rapid onset allowing use as both reliever and preventer in combination inhalers.
entries.uses: Maintenance in asthma (always with an inhaled steroid) and COPD.
entries.cautions: Never use a LABA alone in asthma — mortality risk without concurrent inhaled corticosteroid.

entries.mechanism: Once-daily beta-2 agonism.
entries.uses: COPD maintenance, usually in combination inhalers.
entries.cautions: As other beta-2 agonists.

entries.mechanism: Non-selective phosphodiesterase inhibition raising cAMP, plus adenosine receptor antagonism.
entries.uses: Add-on in severe asthma and COPD; IV aminophylline in life-threatening asthma.
entries.cautions: Narrow therapeutic index — nausea, tremor, arrhythmias, seizures. Levels raised by ciprofloxacin, macrolides and heart failure; lowered by smoking and rifampicin.

entries.mechanism: Adenosine antagonism stimulating the neonatal respiratory centre.
entries.uses: Apnoea of prematurity — improves neurodevelopmental outcome, not merely apnoea count.
entries.cautions: Tachycardia, feeding intolerance; one of the safest drugs in neonatology.

entries.mechanism: Nuclear glucocorticoid receptor agonist — alters gene transcription to suppress airway inflammation over days to weeks.
entries.uses: Preventer therapy in asthma; COPD with exacerbations.
entries.cautions: Oral candidiasis and dysphonia — rinse the mouth and use a spacer; growth and adrenal effects at high dose.

entries.mechanism: As beclometasone, differing in potency and first-pass inactivation.
entries.uses: Asthma and COPD maintenance; budesonide orally for Crohn's and autoimmune hepatitis.
entries.cautions: Fluticasone has high potency and greater systemic absorption at high dose.

entries.mechanism: Blocks cysteinyl-leukotriene type 1 receptors, reducing bronchoconstriction and eosinophilic inflammation.
entries.uses: Add-on in asthma, especially exercise-induced and with allergic rhinitis.
entries.cautions: Neuropsychiatric effects — nightmares, agitation, low mood, including in children — a warning worth giving explicitly.

entries.mechanism: Selective phosphodiesterase-4 inhibition reducing airway inflammation.
entries.uses: Severe COPD with chronic bronchitis and frequent exacerbations.
entries.cautions: Weight loss, diarrhoea, psychiatric effects.

entries.mechanism: Binds free IgE, preventing it engaging mast-cell receptors.
entries.uses: Severe persistent allergic asthma; chronic urticaria.
entries.cautions: Anaphylaxis; injection-site reactions.

entries.mechanism: Block IL-5 or its receptor, depleting the eosinophil population.
entries.uses: Severe eosinophilic asthma; eosinophilic granulomatosis.
entries.cautions: Injection-site reactions; helminth infection risk.

entries.mechanism: Blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signalling, the core of type-2 inflammation.
entries.uses: Severe asthma; atopic eczema; nasal polyps; eosinophilic oesophagitis.
entries.cautions: Transient eosinophilia; conjunctivitis.

entries.mechanism: Block endothelin-1, the most potent endogenous vasoconstrictor, at ET-A and ET-B receptors.
entries.uses: Pulmonary arterial hypertension.
entries.cautions: Hepatotoxicity requiring monthly LFTs (bosentan); anaemia; severely teratogenic. Bosentan induces CYP3A4 and defeats hormonal contraception — a teratogen disabling its own safeguard.

entries.mechanism: Prevent cGMP breakdown in pulmonary vascular smooth muscle, amplifying nitric oxide signalling.
entries.uses: Pulmonary arterial hypertension.
entries.cautions: Absolutely contraindicated with nitrates and with riociguat.

entries.mechanism: Stimulates sGC directly and sensitises it to nitric oxide — a third way into the same pathway.
entries.uses: Pulmonary arterial hypertension; chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.
entries.cautions: Never combine with a PDE5 inhibitor or nitrate; teratogenic.

entries.mechanism: Replace or mimic prostacyclin, giving pulmonary vasodilation and antiproliferative effect.
entries.uses: Severe pulmonary arterial hypertension.
entries.cautions: Epoprostenol has a half-life of minutes and needs a permanent central line — interruption is life-threatening. Jaw pain, flushing, diarrhoea.

entries.mechanism: Reduces fibroblast proliferation and TGF-beta-driven collagen deposition.
entries.uses: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis — slows decline rather than reversing it.
entries.cautions: Photosensitivity requiring strict sun protection, nausea, weight loss, deranged LFTs.

entries.mechanism: Blocks VEGF, FGF and PDGF receptor kinases driving fibroblast signalling.
entries.uses: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; progressive fibrosing ILD; systemic sclerosis ILD.
entries.cautions: Diarrhoea in the majority; bleeding; impaired wound healing — the anti-angiogenic class effects.

entries.mechanism: Reduce sputum viscosity by altering mucus glycoprotein disulfide structure.
entries.uses: COPD with viscid sputum; bronchiectasis.
entries.cautions: GI upset; avoid in active peptic ulceration.

entries.mechanism: Cleaves extracellular DNA from degraded neutrophils, thinning cystic fibrosis sputum.
entries.uses: Cystic fibrosis.
entries.cautions: Voice change, pharyngitis.

entries.mechanism: Correct folding and potentiate gating of the defective CFTR chloride channel — disease-modifying rather than symptomatic.
entries.uses: Cystic fibrosis with responsive genotypes.
entries.cautions: Hepatotoxicity, cataracts; requires genotype testing first.

entries.mechanism: Replace the phospholipid that lowers alveolar surface tension, which preterm lungs cannot yet make — instilled directly into the trachea.
entries.uses: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
entries.cautions: Transient bradycardia and desaturation during instillation; pulmonary haemorrhage.

entries.mechanism: Suppresses the medullary cough centre through sigma-1 and NMDA actions without opioid analgesia.
entries.uses: Dry cough; with bupropion for depression.
entries.cautions: Serotonin syndrome with SSRIs and MAOIs; dissociative effects and misuse at high dose — unexpected for a cough medicine.

entries.mechanism: Anaesthetises stretch receptors in the lung and pleura, damping the cough reflex at its origin.
entries.uses: Symptomatic cough.
entries.cautions: Fatal in overdose in children; capsules must be swallowed whole — chewing causes oropharyngeal anaesthesia and choking.

entries.mechanism: Increases respiratory tract fluid volume, thinning secretions to make cough more productive.
entries.uses: Productive cough, usually in combination products.
entries.cautions: Weak evidence base; nausea at high dose.

entries.mechanism: Vasoconstrict nasal mucosal vessels locally.
entries.uses: Short-term nasal congestion.
entries.cautions: Rhinitis medicamentosa — rebound congestion after about five days of use.

entries.mechanism: Block peripheral histamine H1 receptors; poor blood-brain barrier penetration keeps them largely non-sedating.
entries.uses: Allergic rhinitis, urticaria, allergic conjunctivitis.
entries.cautions: Mild sedation with cetirizine; the driving-safe choice over older agents.

entries.mechanism: As cetirizine; fexofenadine is the least sedating.
entries.uses: Allergic rhinitis, urticaria.
entries.cautions: Fexofenadine absorption reduced by fruit juice and antacids.

entries.mechanism: Crosses into the CNS and also blocks muscarinic receptors — hence sedation and antimuscarinic effects.
entries.uses: Acute allergic reactions; pruritus; sedation.
entries.cautions: Drowsiness, dry mouth, urinary retention; avoid in the elderly.

entries.mechanism: H1 and muscarinic blockade with marked CNS penetration.
entries.uses: Allergy; insomnia; acute dystonia; motion sickness.
entries.cautions: Anticholinergic delirium in the elderly; deliriant misuse at high dose; the basis of most OTC sleep aids.

entries.mechanism: H1 blockade with anxiolytic and antiemetic action.
entries.uses: Anxiety, pruritus, sedation, nausea.
entries.cautions: Dose-dependent QT prolongation; sedation.

entries.mechanism: H1 blockade with strong antimuscarinic, antidopaminergic and sedative actions.
entries.uses: Nausea and motion sickness; sedation; allergy.
entries.cautions: Marked sedation; extrapyramidal effects; severe tissue injury on extravasation; not for children under two.

entries.mechanism: Block H1 and muscarinic receptors in the vestibular nuclei and vomiting centre.
entries.uses: Motion sickness, vertigo, labyrinthitis; nausea in palliative care.
entries.cautions: Sedation and anticholinergic effects; used beyond a few days they impair central vestibular compensation and prolong the symptom.

entries.mechanism: Local H1 blockade with mast-cell stabilising action.
entries.uses: Allergic rhinitis (nasal spray); allergic conjunctivitis (drops).
entries.cautions: Bitter taste with nasal azelastine; local irritation.

entries.mechanism: Prevents mast-cell degranulation rather than blocking histamine after release.
entries.uses: Allergic conjunctivitis and rhinitis; mastocytosis.
entries.cautions: Must be used prophylactically and regularly to work at all.

entries.mechanism: A prodrug activated in the acidic canaliculus that irreversibly inhibits the gastric H+/K+-ATPase — the final common step of acid secretion, so it outperforms every upstream blocker.
entries.uses: GORD, peptic ulcer, H. pylori eradication, NSAID ulcer prophylaxis, upper GI bleeding.
entries.cautions: Headache, diarrhoea; long term — hypomagnesaemia, B12 deficiency, fracture risk, C. difficile and microscopic colitis. Inhibits CYP2C19.

entries.mechanism: As omeprazole; pantoprazole has the fewest CYP interactions.
entries.uses: As omeprazole.
entries.cautions: Same class profile.

entries.mechanism: Blocks histamine H2 receptors on the gastric parietal cell — upstream of the pump, hence less complete than a PPI.
entries.uses: GORD and dyspepsia; night-time adjunct to PPI therapy.
entries.cautions: Generally well tolerated. Ranitidine was withdrawn worldwide in 2020 over NDMA contamination.

entries.mechanism: Chemically neutralise gastric acid; alginates form a floating raft that physically blocks reflux.
entries.uses: Symptomatic relief of heartburn and dyspepsia.
entries.cautions: Fast but short-lived. Magnesium salts loosen, aluminium salts constipate; they bind other drugs.

entries.mechanism: Forms a viscous adherent barrier over ulcer craters in acid conditions.
entries.uses: Ulcer healing; stress-ulcer prophylaxis; oral mucositis.
entries.cautions: Binds other drugs; needs an acid environment so it clashes with PPIs.

entries.mechanism: Replaces the protective prostaglandins that NSAIDs suppress, restoring mucus and bicarbonate.
entries.uses: NSAID ulcer prophylaxis; obstetric use for induction, miscarriage and post-partum haemorrhage.
entries.cautions: Diarrhoea; a potent uterotonic — contraindicated in pregnancy for GI indications.

entries.mechanism: Blocks serotonin receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone and on vagal afferents in the gut.
entries.uses: Chemotherapy-and radiotherapy-induced nausea; post-operative nausea; gastroenteritis in children.
entries.cautions: Constipation and headache; QT prolongation; avoid in early pregnancy (small cleft-palate signal).

entries.mechanism: Central dopamine blockade at the chemoreceptor trigger zone plus a peripheral prokinetic effect speeding gastric emptying.
entries.uses: Nausea in gastroparesis, migraine and post-operatively.
entries.cautions: Extrapyramidal reactions — acute dystonia especially in young women; avoid in bowel obstruction and Parkinson's. Short courses only.

entries.mechanism: Blocks dopamine receptors but crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly, so far fewer movement effects.
entries.uses: Nausea in Parkinson's disease; gastroparesis; lactation induction.
entries.cautions: QT prolongation and sudden cardiac death — short courses and lowest dose only.

entries.mechanism: Central dopamine blockade in the vomiting pathways.
entries.uses: Vertigo, labyrinthine nausea, vomiting.
entries.cautions: Sedation, extrapyramidal effects, postural hypotension.

entries.mechanism: Block neurokinin-1 receptors in the vomiting centre — a distinct pathway from serotonin.
entries.uses: Delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea, with a 5-HT3 antagonist and dexamethasone.
entries.cautions: CYP3A4 interactions including with dexamethasone and contraceptives.

entries.mechanism: Retain water in the stool, increasing bulk and stimulating peristalsis.
entries.uses: Constipation; IBS; diverticular disease.
entries.cautions: Must be taken with plenty of fluid; avoid in obstruction or faecal impaction.

entries.mechanism: Draw water into the bowel lumen osmotically; lactulose is additionally fermented to acids that trap ammonia.
entries.uses: Constipation; bowel preparation; lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy.
entries.cautions: Bloating, flatulence, cramps; electrolyte shifts with high-volume macrogol.

entries.mechanism: Directly stimulate the enteric nerves to increase motility and secretion.
entries.uses: Constipation, particularly opioid-related; bowel preparation.
entries.cautions: Cramping; avoid in obstruction.

entries.mechanism: Surfactant that lets water penetrate the stool.
entries.uses: Constipation, especially where straining is a hazard.
entries.cautions: Modest efficacy; often combined with senna.

entries.mechanism: Raises intestinal cGMP, increasing chloride and fluid secretion into the lumen and reducing visceral pain signalling.
entries.uses: Irritable bowel syndrome with constipation.
entries.cautions: Diarrhoea is dose-limiting; contraindicated in children.

entries.mechanism: Stimulates colonic 5-HT4 receptors to increase propulsive motility; selectivity avoids the cardiac problems that withdrew cisapride.
entries.uses: Chronic constipation unresponsive to laxatives.
entries.cautions: Headache, nausea, diarrhoea.

entries.mechanism: Exploits the intact sodium-glucose cotransporter in the gut to drive water absorption even during secretory diarrhoea — arguably the highest-impact formulation in global health.
entries.uses: Dehydration from diarrhoeal illness.
entries.cautions: Must be reconstituted with the correct water volume.

entries.mechanism: Restores enterocyte function and mucosal immunity, shortening diarrhoeal episodes and reducing recurrence.
entries.uses: Childhood diarrhoea, alongside oral rehydration salts.
entries.cautions: Vomiting at higher doses; a cheap, high-impact intervention.

entries.mechanism: Topical anti-inflammatory action on colonic mucosa; mechanism incompletely defined.
entries.uses: Induction and maintenance of remission in ulcerative colitis.
entries.cautions: Renal impairment (monitor), pancreatitis, blood dyscrasias.

entries.mechanism: Split by colonic bacteria into 5-ASA (gut action) and sulfapyridine (systemic immunomodulation).
entries.uses: Ulcerative colitis; rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis.
entries.cautions: Rash, nausea, reversible oligospermia, orange body fluids; marrow suppression.

entries.mechanism: Neutralise tumour necrosis factor, a master switch of inflammation.
entries.uses: Moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
entries.cautions: Infection and TB reactivation — screen before starting; loss of response from anti-drug antibodies.

entries.mechanism: Vedolizumab blocks alpha-4-beta-7 integrin so lymphocytes cannot enter gut tissue; ustekinumab blocks the shared p40 subunit.
entries.uses: Inflammatory bowel disease.
entries.cautions: Vedolizumab's gut selectivity gives a favourable infection profile.

entries.mechanism: Rifampicin-class RNA polymerase inhibition, but essentially unabsorbed, so it acts only on gut flora.
entries.uses: Prevention of recurrent hepatic encephalopathy; travellers' diarrhoea; IBS with diarrhoea.
entries.cautions: Minimal systemic effects by design; expensive.

entries.mechanism: Displaces toxic hydrophobic bile acids and improves bile flow.
entries.uses: Primary biliary cholangitis; cholestasis of pregnancy.
entries.cautions: Diarrhoea; ineffective for most gallstones.

entries.mechanism: Supplies lipase, amylase and protease for digestion.
entries.uses: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency; cystic fibrosis.
entries.cautions: Take with food; high doses linked to fibrosing colonopathy in children.

entries.mechanism: Lowers surface tension of gas bubbles so they coalesce and pass — a purely physical action, with no absorption at all.
entries.uses: Flatulence, infant colic, bowel preparation adjunct.
entries.cautions: Essentially inert; efficacy modest.

entries.mechanism: Splanchnic vasoconstriction reduces portal venous inflow and hence portal pressure.
entries.uses: Variceal haemorrhage; hepatorenal syndrome.
entries.cautions: Peripheral, cardiac and mesenteric ischaemia; hyponatraemia.

entries.mechanism: Modified to precipitate or bind albumin, giving a flat 24-hour profile that mimics basal secretion.
entries.uses: Basal cover in type 1 and advanced type 2 diabetes.
entries.cautions: Hypoglycaemia; weight gain; lipohypertrophy at injection sites. Degludec is the flattest and longest.

entries.mechanism: Amino-acid substitutions prevent hexamer formation, so absorption is fast enough to cover a meal.
entries.uses: Prandial cover; insulin pumps; diabetic ketoacidosis (IV).
entries.cautions: Hypoglycaemia if the meal is missed after dosing.

entries.mechanism: Unmodified human sequence; isophane is complexed with protamine to slow absorption.
entries.uses: Where analogues are unaffordable; twice-daily mixed regimens.
entries.cautions: Less predictable profile than analogues; nocturnal hypoglycaemia with isophane.

entries.mechanism: Reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves peripheral insulin sensitivity; crucially it does not stimulate insulin release, so alone it does not cause hypoglycaemia.
entries.uses: First-line for type 2 diabetes; polycystic ovary syndrome.
entries.cautions: GI upset and metallic taste; B12 depletion over years; rare lactic acidosis — withheld in significant renal impairment and around iodinated contrast.

entries.mechanism: Closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels on beta cells, depolarising them and forcing insulin release regardless of glucose level.
entries.uses: Type 2 diabetes when metformin is insufficient; useful where rapid symptom relief is needed.
entries.cautions: Hypoglycaemia and weight gain — the opposite profile to metformin, and the reason the patient must now be counselled about hypos.

entries.mechanism: As gliclazide, with longer duration.
entries.uses: Type 2 diabetes.
entries.cautions: Greater and more prolonged hypoglycaemia, particularly in the elderly and in renal impairment; glibenclamide unsuitable over 60.

entries.mechanism: Close the same beta-cell potassium channel as sulfonylureas but at a different binding site, with fast onset and short duration — taken with each meal and skipped if the meal is skipped.
entries.uses: Type 2 diabetes with erratic meal patterns.
entries.cautions: Hypoglycaemia (less than sulfonylureas); gemfibrozil raises repaglinide levels dangerously.

entries.mechanism: Block dipeptidyl peptidase-4, so endogenous incretins survive longer to stimulate glucose-dependent insulin release.
entries.uses: Type 2 diabetes, second-or third-line; linagliptin needs no renal dose adjustment.
entries.cautions: Weight-neutral with low hypoglycaemia risk; pancreatitis (rare); arthralgia; bullous pemphigoid.

entries.mechanism: Mimics incretin GLP-1 — boosts glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying and reduces appetite centrally.
entries.uses: Type 2 diabetes; obesity; cardiovascular risk reduction.
entries.cautions: Nausea and vomiting on titration; gallstones; pancreatitis; delayed gastric emptying matters for anaesthesia. Contraindicated with medullary thyroid carcinoma history.

entries.mechanism: As semaglutide, differing in dosing interval.
entries.uses: Type 2 diabetes; obesity (liraglutide).
entries.cautions: Same GI and pancreatic profile.

entries.class: Dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist
entries.mechanism: Adds GIP receptor agonism to GLP-1, producing greater glycaemic and weight effect than either alone.
entries.uses: Type 2 diabetes; obesity.
entries.cautions: As the GLP-1 agonists, with more marked GI effects at higher doses.

entries.mechanism: Block the sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 in the proximal tubule, so glucose is excreted in urine; independently they protect heart and kidney.
entries.uses: Type 2 diabetes; heart failure across the ejection-fraction range; chronic kidney disease.
entries.cautions: Genital and urinary infection (the urine now contains sugar); volume depletion; rare euglycaemic ketoacidosis — which catches clinicians out because glucose looks normal. Canagliflozin: amputation signal.

entries.mechanism: Activates PPAR-gamma, altering gene transcription to improve peripheral insulin sensitivity.
entries.uses: Type 2 diabetes with marked insulin resistance; NASH.
entries.cautions: Fluid retention and heart failure; weight gain; fracture risk; bladder cancer signal.

entries.mechanism: Delays intestinal carbohydrate digestion, blunting post-prandial glucose peaks.
entries.uses: Type 2 diabetes, chiefly post-prandial hyperglycaemia.
entries.cautions: Flatulence and diarrhoea limit use; hypoglycaemia must be treated with glucose, not sucrose, since sucrose cannot be split.

entries.mechanism: Raises hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, releasing glucose.
entries.uses: Severe hypoglycaemia without IV access; beta-blocker overdose (raises cardiac cAMP bypassing the blocked receptor).
entries.cautions: Ineffective if glycogen stores are depleted (alcohol, starvation); nausea and vomiting.

entries.mechanism: Opens the beta-cell potassium channel — the exact opposite of a sulfonylurea — so insulin secretion is suppressed.
entries.uses: Persistent hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia of infancy; insulinoma.
entries.cautions: Fluid retention, hypertrichosis, hyperglycaemia.

entries.mechanism: Central appetite suppression through hypothalamic GLP-1 receptors, plus delayed gastric emptying.
entries.uses: Obesity and weight management.
entries.cautions: Nausea during titration; gallstones; weight regain on stopping — it treats rather than cures.

entries.mechanism: Blocks lipase in the gut lumen so about a third of dietary fat passes undigested; it never enters the circulation.
entries.uses: Obesity alongside a reduced-fat diet.
entries.cautions: Steatorrhoea and oily leakage proportional to dietary fat — effectively enforcing adherence; reduces fat-soluble vitamin absorption.

entries.mechanism: Releases hypothalamic noradrenaline, suppressing appetite.
entries.uses: Short-term weight management (mainly US).
entries.cautions: Hypertension, palpitations, insomnia, dependence; the survivor of a drug class largely withdrawn for cardiac and psychiatric harm.

entries.mechanism: Bupropion stimulates hypothalamic POMC neurons; naltrexone removes the opioid-mediated brake on them.
entries.uses: Obesity management.
entries.cautions: Raised blood pressure, seizures, nausea; contraindicated with opioids.

entries.mechanism: Replaces deficient hormone; converted peripherally to active T3, restoring metabolic rate.
entries.uses: Hypothyroidism; suppression after thyroid cancer.
