entries.cautions: Over-replacement causes palpitations, tremor, weight loss, atrial fibrillation, bone loss. Absorption reduced by calcium, iron and PPIs — take on an empty stomach.

entries.mechanism: Directly supplies T3 with rapid onset.
entries.uses: Myxoedema coma; occasional adjunct.
entries.cautions: Narrow margin and short half-life; cardiac risk in the elderly.

entries.mechanism: Block thyroid peroxidase and hence hormone synthesis; carbimazole is the prodrug of methimazole.
entries.uses: Hyperthyroidism including Graves' disease.
entries.cautions: Rare but critical agranulocytosis — report sore throat or fever urgently for an immediate blood count. Teratogenic in the first trimester.

entries.mechanism: Blocks thyroid peroxidase and also peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion.
entries.uses: First trimester of pregnancy; thyroid storm.
entries.cautions: Hepatotoxicity (can be fulminant) and ANCA vasculitis — hence second-line.

entries.mechanism: In pharmacological excess it transiently blocks hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff effect) and saturates the thyroid against radioiodine uptake.
entries.uses: Thyroid storm; pre-operative preparation; thyroid blocking after radiation release.
entries.cautions: Only transient in thyrotoxicosis — escape occurs within days; iodism with prolonged use.

entries.mechanism: Concentrated by the sodium-iodide symporter, which the thyroid has and almost nothing else does; beta emission then destroys the follicular cells. Selectivity here is anatomical, not molecular.
entries.uses: Hyperthyroidism; ablation after thyroid cancer surgery.
entries.cautions: Permanent hypothyroidism is the expected outcome, not a failure; contraindicated in pregnancy; contact restrictions afterwards.

entries.mechanism: Enters the cell and alters gene transcription, producing anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressant effects that take hours to appear.
entries.uses: Asthma and COPD exacerbations, autoimmune and inflammatory disease, transplant, some cancers.
entries.cautions: Long term — weight gain and moon face, hyperglycaemia, thin skin, osteoporosis, infection, mood change, hypertension, cataracts. Never stop abruptly: taper to avoid adrenal crisis.

entries.mechanism: Converted to prednisolone by hepatic 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase — so it is ineffective in significant liver failure.
entries.uses: As prednisolone (the standard oral steroid in US practice).
entries.cautions: As prednisolone.

entries.mechanism: Mimics endogenous cortisol closely, so it suits physiological replacement.
entries.uses: Adrenal insufficiency replacement and sick-day dosing; acute severe asthma and anaphylaxis adjunct.
entries.cautions: As prednisolone; more salt and water retention.

entries.mechanism: As prednisolone with greater potency; high-dose pulses for severe inflammation.
entries.uses: MS relapse, transplant rejection, severe vasculitis, intra-articular injection.
entries.cautions: Hyperglycaemia, mood disturbance, infection; pulses may cause flushing and arrhythmia.

entries.mechanism: Very high glucocorticoid potency with negligible mineralocorticoid effect.
entries.uses: Cerebral oedema, croup, chemotherapy antiemesis, severe COVID-19, fetal lung maturation, dexamethasone suppression testing.
entries.cautions: Marked hyperglycaemia, insomnia, agitation; prolonged HPA suppression.

entries.mechanism: As dexamethasone; depot formulations for intra-articular and intramuscular use.
entries.uses: Joint injection, allergic rhinitis, dermatology, fetal lung maturation.
entries.cautions: Local tissue atrophy; crystal-induced flare after injection.

entries.mechanism: Potent aldosterone-receptor agonist promoting sodium and water retention.
entries.uses: Addison's disease (with hydrocortisone); severe orthostatic hypotension.
entries.cautions: Hypertension, hypokalaemia, oedema.

entries.mechanism: Block adrenal cortisol synthesis enzymes.
entries.uses: Medical control of Cushing's syndrome.
entries.cautions: Adrenal insufficiency; ketoconazole is hepatotoxic and a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor.

entries.mechanism: Dopamine is the physiological inhibitor of prolactin, so a D2 agonist switches prolactin off and shrinks lactotroph tumours.
entries.uses: Prolactinoma; hyperprolactinaemia; acromegaly adjunct; suppression of lactation.
entries.cautions: Nausea, postural hypotension; cardiac valve fibrosis at high cumulative dose; impulse-control disorders.

entries.mechanism: Mimic somatostatin, the hypothalamic inhibitor of growth hormone release.
entries.uses: Acromegaly; neuroendocrine tumours; carcinoid syndrome; variceal bleeding.
entries.cautions: Gallstones, hyperglycaemia, steatorrhoea.

entries.mechanism: Blocks the GH receptor peripherally, so IGF-1 falls even though GH rises — meaning GH can no longer be used to monitor the disease.
entries.uses: Acromegaly refractory to somatostatin analogues.
entries.cautions: Hepatotoxicity; tumour size must be monitored separately by imaging.

entries.mechanism: Replaces GH, acting largely through hepatic IGF-1.
entries.uses: GH deficiency; Turner and Prader-Willi syndromes.
entries.cautions: Intracranial hypertension, slipped upper femoral epiphysis, insulin resistance.

entries.mechanism: Selective antidiuresis without vasoconstriction.
entries.uses: Cranial diabetes insipidus; nocturnal enuresis.
entries.cautions: Hyponatraemia — fluid restriction and sodium monitoring.

entries.drug: Combined oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel, norethisterone, norgestimate, desogestrel or drospirenone)
entries.mechanism: Suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary drive that triggers ovulation, thickens cervical mucus and thins the endometrium.
entries.uses: Contraception; menstrual regulation; acne; endometriosis.
entries.cautions: Venous thromboembolism risk driven mainly by the oestrogen — avoid with clotting risk, migraine with aura, or smoking over 35. The classic victim of enzyme induction: rifampicin, carbamazepine and St John's Wort cause failure.

entries.mechanism: Thickens cervical mucus and thins endometrium; desogestrel also inhibits ovulation.
entries.uses: Contraception where oestrogen is contraindicated; breastfeeding.
entries.cautions: Irregular bleeding is the commonest reason for stopping; much less clot risk.

entries.mechanism: Delay or inhibit ovulation; ineffective once ovulation has occurred.
entries.uses: Emergency contraception.
entries.cautions: Ulipristal works later in the cycle but is reduced by recent progestogen; both less effective at higher body weight.

entries.drug: Depot medroxyprogesterone / etonogestrel implant / levonorgestrel IUS / norelgestromin patch
entries.mechanism: Sustained progestogen exposure suppressing ovulation or acting locally on the endometrium.
entries.uses: Long-acting contraception; menorrhagia (IUS).
entries.cautions: Delayed return of fertility with the injection; bone density loss with prolonged depot use.

entries.mechanism: Replaces declining oestrogen; a progestogen is added if the uterus is present to protect the endometrium.
entries.uses: Menopausal vasomotor symptoms, urogenital atrophy, premature ovarian insufficiency.
entries.cautions: VTE risk (lower transdermal), stroke, breast cancer with combined preparations — balance depends on age and time since menopause.

entries.mechanism: Endometrial protection and luteal support.
entries.uses: HRT with oestrogen; luteal phase support in IVF; preterm birth prevention.
entries.cautions: Sedation (taken at night); dizziness.

entries.class: Synthetic steroid with oestrogenic, progestogenic and androgenic activity
entries.mechanism: Metabolites act differently in different tissues, giving endometrial protection without a separate progestogen.
entries.uses: Menopausal symptoms and bone protection.
entries.cautions: Stroke risk in older women; breast cancer recurrence.

entries.mechanism: Blocks hypothalamic oestrogen receptors so the brain perceives low oestrogen and increases FSH, driving ovulation.
entries.uses: Anovulatory infertility, including polycystic ovary syndrome.
entries.cautions: Multiple pregnancy; ovarian hyperstimulation; visual disturbance.

entries.mechanism: Lowers oestrogen so the same negative-feedback release drives FSH — now often preferred to clomifene in PCOS.
entries.uses: Ovulation induction.
entries.cautions: Multiple pregnancy; off-label in many jurisdictions.

entries.mechanism: Directly stimulate follicular development and trigger ovulation, bypassing the pituitary entirely.
entries.uses: Assisted reproduction; hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism.
entries.cautions: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome — potentially life-threatening; multiple pregnancy.

entries.mechanism: Immediately block pituitary GnRH receptors without the initial flare that agonists cause.
entries.uses: Preventing premature LH surge in IVF cycles.
entries.cautions: Injection-site reactions.

entries.mechanism: Stimulates rhythmic uterine contraction and milk let-down.
entries.uses: Induction and augmentation of labour; prevention and treatment of post-partum haemorrhage.
entries.cautions: Uterine hyperstimulation and fetal distress; water intoxication with high-dose infusion.

entries.mechanism: Sustained uterotonic effect from a single dose; the heat-stable formulation needs no cold chain.
entries.uses: Prevention of post-partum haemorrhage, especially where refrigeration is unreliable.
entries.cautions: As oxytocin.

entries.mechanism: Sustained uterine contraction via serotonergic and adrenergic receptors.
entries.uses: Post-partum haemorrhage, often combined with oxytocin.
entries.cautions: Marked nausea and vomiting; hypertension — avoid in pre-eclampsia.

entries.mechanism: Nifedipine relaxes myometrium via calcium-channel blockade; atosiban is an oxytocin receptor antagonist.
entries.uses: Delaying preterm labour to allow steroids and transfer.
entries.cautions: Maternal hypotension and flushing with nifedipine.

entries.mechanism: Mifepristone blocks progesterone support of the pregnancy and sensitises the myometrium; misoprostol then produces contractions.
entries.uses: Medical termination of pregnancy; management of miscarriage and intrauterine fetal demise.
entries.cautions: Bleeding, cramping, infection; legal restrictions vary widely by jurisdiction.

entries.mechanism: Binds fetal RhD-positive cells in the maternal circulation before her immune system can mount a response — preventing sensitisation rather than treating it.
entries.uses: RhD-negative mothers after delivery or sensitising events.
entries.cautions: Useless once alloimmunisation has already occurred; timing is everything.

entries.mechanism: Maintains patency of the ductus arteriosus, preserving mixing until surgery — the exact opposite of indometacin's use.
entries.uses: Duct-dependent congenital heart disease in neonates.
entries.cautions: Apnoea (be ready to ventilate), hypotension, fever.

entries.mechanism: Ripens the cervix and stimulates uterine contraction.
entries.uses: Induction of labour.
entries.cautions: Uterine hyperstimulation; avoid after previous caesarean.

entries.mechanism: Replaces endogenous androgen, restoring secondary sexual characteristics, libido, muscle and bone mass.
entries.uses: Male hypogonadism; gender-affirming hormone therapy.
entries.cautions: Polycythaemia, acne, sleep apnoea, suppression of spermatogenesis; prostate monitoring. Controlled drug in many countries.

entries.mechanism: Block conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, shrinking the prostate over months.
entries.uses: Benign prostatic hyperplasia; male-pattern hair loss.
entries.cautions: Reduced libido and erectile dysfunction, sometimes persistent; halves PSA — remember when interpreting results. Teratogenic to a male fetus.

entries.mechanism: Block phosphodiesterase-5, so cGMP accumulates in the corpus cavernosum and pulmonary vasculature, producing vasodilation.
entries.uses: Erectile dysfunction; pulmonary arterial hypertension; tadalafil also for BPH.
entries.cautions: Absolutely contraindicated with nitrates. Headache, flushing, blue-tinged vision (PDE6 cross-reactivity); rare non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.

entries.mechanism: Continuous rather than pulsatile GnRH stimulation paradoxically downregulates pituitary receptors, shutting off gonadal steroid production.
entries.uses: Prostate cancer; endometriosis; breast cancer; precocious puberty.
entries.cautions: Initial testosterone flare — cover with an antiandrogen; hot flushes, bone loss.

entries.mechanism: Binds hydroxyapatite and is taken up by osteoclasts, inhibiting them and slowing bone resorption.
entries.uses: Osteoporosis; steroid-induced bone loss; Paget's disease.
entries.cautions: Poor oral absorption and oesophageal irritation — empty stomach, full glass of water, sit upright. Rare osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fracture.

entries.mechanism: As alendronate, delivered as an annual infusion.
entries.uses: Osteoporosis; hypercalcaemia of malignancy; bone metastases.
entries.cautions: Acute-phase flu-like reaction after the first infusion; renal impairment; dental check first.

entries.mechanism: Blocks RANK ligand, preventing osteoclast formation — a different route to the same end as bisphosphonates.
entries.uses: Osteoporosis; skeletal events in bone metastases.
entries.cautions: Hypocalcaemia; rebound vertebral fractures if stopped without follow-on therapy — it must never simply be discontinued.

entries.mechanism: Intermittent parathyroid hormone exposure paradoxically stimulates osteoblasts, uniquely building new bone rather than slowing loss.
entries.uses: Severe osteoporosis with fractures.
entries.cautions: Hypercalcaemia; limited treatment duration.

entries.mechanism: Blocks sclerostin, simultaneously increasing bone formation and reducing resorption.
entries.uses: Severe postmenopausal osteoporosis.
entries.cautions: Cardiovascular events — avoid after MI or stroke.

entries.mechanism: Oestrogen agonist in bone, antagonist in breast, neutral in uterus.
entries.uses: Postmenopausal osteoporosis; breast cancer risk reduction.
entries.cautions: VTE risk; hot flushes.

entries.mechanism: Supply the raw material for bone and enable its absorption from the gut.
entries.uses: Underpins all osteoporosis treatment; vitamin D deficiency; rickets; hypocalcaemia.
entries.cautions: Constipation and hypercalcaemia at high dose; calcium binds levothyroxine, bisphosphonates and tetracyclines.

entries.mechanism: Bypass the failed renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation step, supplying already-active hormone.
entries.uses: Renal bone disease; hypoparathyroidism; severe hypocalcaemia.
entries.cautions: Hypercalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia; monitor calcium.

entries.mechanism: Directly inhibits osteoclasts and lowers serum calcium — the physiological counterweight to parathyroid hormone.
entries.uses: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy (rapid but short-lived); Paget's disease; acute vertebral fracture pain.
entries.cautions: Tachyphylaxis within days as receptors downregulate; nasal formulation withdrawn in some countries over cancer signal.

entries.mechanism: Increases the parathyroid receptor's sensitivity to calcium, suppressing PTH release.
entries.uses: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in dialysis; parathyroid carcinoma.
entries.cautions: Hypocalcaemia; nausea.

entries.mechanism: Does not open the chloride channel itself; it enhances GABA's own effect, making neurons harder to fire. Long half-life with active metabolites.
entries.uses: Acute severe anxiety, alcohol withdrawal, muscle spasm, status epilepticus (rectal or IV).
entries.cautions: Sedation, falls, dependence and tolerance — short-term use only; dangerous respiratory depression with opioids or alcohol; taper to avoid withdrawal seizures. Antidote: flumazenil.

entries.mechanism: As diazepam; intermediate half-life with no active metabolites, so more predictable in the elderly and in liver disease.
entries.uses: Status epilepticus, acute agitation, pre-medication, alcohol withdrawal in liver disease.
entries.cautions: As diazepam; the preferred parenteral agent for seizures.

entries.mechanism: Rapid onset and offset; water-soluble at low pH, lipophilic at body pH.
entries.uses: Procedural sedation; buccal route for seizures in the community; palliative care.
entries.cautions: Profound respiratory depression, especially with opioids.

entries.mechanism: High-potency GABA-A modulation with fast onset.
entries.uses: Panic disorder (US practice).
entries.cautions: The fast onset and short duration make it the most reinforcing and most misused benzodiazepine; severe interdose rebound anxiety.

entries.mechanism: Sustained GABA-A modulation.
entries.uses: Myoclonic and cluster seizures; panic disorder; adjunct in epilepsy.
entries.cautions: Tolerance to the antiseizure effect develops; sedation.

entries.mechanism: GABA-A modulation with a duration suited to sleep.
entries.uses: Short-term insomnia.
entries.cautions: Hangover sedation, dependence; two-to-four-week limit.

entries.mechanism: Act at the same benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor despite the different chemistry and name.
entries.uses: Short-term insomnia.
entries.cautions: Identical dependence concerns to benzodiazepines; complex sleep behaviours (sleep-driving, sleep-eating); metallic taste with zopiclone.

entries.mechanism: Substitutes for the GABAergic tone alcohol was providing, preventing rebound excitation.
entries.uses: Managed alcohol withdrawal, as a reducing regimen.
entries.cautions: Over-sedation; accumulates in liver disease — lorazepam preferred there.

entries.mechanism: Enhances GABA-A by prolonging channel opening, and at higher concentrations opens the channel directly — unlike benzodiazepines there is no ceiling, which is why overdose is lethal.
entries.uses: Seizures and status epilepticus, especially neonatal; still the most-used antiseizure drug worldwide on cost grounds.
entries.cautions: Sedation, cognitive and behavioural effects in children, dependence; a powerful enzyme inducer. Narrow therapeutic index.

entries.mechanism: Mimics the endogenous circadian sleep signal.
entries.uses: Insomnia in the elderly; jet lag; sleep disorders in neurodevelopmental conditions.
entries.cautions: Daytime drowsiness; no dependence.

entries.mechanism: Block orexin, the neuropeptide that maintains wakefulness — removing the wake signal rather than sedating.
entries.uses: Chronic insomnia.
entries.cautions: Next-day somnolence; sleep paralysis; avoid in narcolepsy, where orexin is already deficient.

entries.mechanism: Non-sedating anxiolysis over weeks, without GABA involvement.
entries.uses: Generalised anxiety disorder.
entries.cautions: Slow onset makes it useless as a rescue medicine; dizziness, nausea.

entries.mechanism: Competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A.
entries.uses: Reversal of benzodiazepine sedation or overdose.
entries.cautions: Precipitates seizures in dependent users and in mixed overdose with tricyclics — used cautiously and rarely.

entries.mechanism: Blocks the serotonin transporter; benefit builds over weeks as adaptive changes follow.
entries.uses: Depression (first-line), anxiety disorders, OCD, PTSD; preferred after MI.
entries.cautions: Early nausea, headache, sexual dysfunction, initial anxiety increase; hyponatraemia in the elderly; bleeding tendency; discontinuation symptoms. Benefit takes 2–4 weeks — counselling prevents early abandonment.

entries.mechanism: As sertraline; very long half-life through its active metabolite.
entries.uses: Depression, bulimia, OCD; the SSRI with most evidence in adolescents.
entries.cautions: Long half-life makes discontinuation mild but interactions persist for weeks; CYP2D6 inhibitor.

entries.mechanism: As sertraline; escitalopram is the active enantiomer.
entries.uses: Depression, panic disorder, generalised anxiety.
entries.cautions: Dose-dependent QT prolongation — maximum doses capped, more strictly in the elderly.

entries.mechanism: As sertraline; short half-life and potent CYP2D6 inhibition.
entries.uses: Depression, anxiety, OCD.
entries.cautions: Worst discontinuation syndrome of the class; most anticholinergic; avoid in pregnancy.

entries.mechanism: As sertraline; potent CYP1A2 inhibitor.
entries.uses: OCD; depression.
entries.cautions: Raises theophylline, clozapine and caffeine levels substantially.

entries.mechanism: Block both transporters; noradrenergic effects appear at higher doses.
entries.uses: Depression, generalised anxiety, menopausal flushing.
entries.cautions: Raise blood pressure; marked discontinuation symptoms; more dangerous in overdose than SSRIs.

entries.mechanism: Balanced serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibition.
entries.uses: Depression; diabetic neuropathic pain; stress incontinence; fibromyalgia.
entries.cautions: Hepatotoxicity; raises blood pressure; discontinuation symptoms.

entries.mechanism: Blocks presynaptic alpha-2 autoreceptors (increasing monoamine release) plus 5-HT2, 5-HT3 and H1 receptors.
entries.uses: Depression, particularly with insomnia and poor appetite.
entries.cautions: Sedation and weight gain — often why it is chosen; sedation is greater at low dose; rare agranulocytosis.

entries.mechanism: Raises dopaminergic and noradrenergic tone with no serotonergic action — hence no sexual dysfunction.
entries.uses: Depression; smoking cessation; adjunct in obesity.
entries.cautions: Lowers seizure threshold — avoid in epilepsy, eating disorders and alcohol withdrawal; insomnia, agitation.

entries.mechanism: Weak serotonin reuptake inhibition with strong 5-HT2 and H1 antagonism — the antihistamine effect dominates at the low doses actually prescribed.
entries.uses: Insomnia (predominant real-world use); depression at higher doses.
entries.cautions: Sedation, postural hypotension, priapism (rare but a urological emergency); QT prolongation.

entries.mechanism: Blocks serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake, plus muscarinic, histamine and alpha-1 receptors — and it is that extra, unwanted blockade that produces the side-effect profile.
entries.uses: Now mainly low-dose for neuropathic pain, migraine prophylaxis and insomnia.
entries.cautions: Anticholinergic set, sedation, postural hypotension, and lethality in overdose from arrhythmia and seizures — the main reason SSRIs are preferred.

entries.mechanism: Secondary amine with less anticholinergic and sedative burden than amitriptyline.
entries.uses: Depression; neuropathic pain.
entries.cautions: Best tolerated TCA but same overdose hazard.

entries.mechanism: The most serotonergic of the tricyclics.
entries.uses: Obsessive-compulsive disorder — still a reference standard; depression.
entries.cautions: Anticholinergic effects; seizures at high dose; overdose hazard.

entries.mechanism: As amitriptyline with varying anticholinergic burden.
entries.uses: Depression; nocturnal enuresis (imipramine).
entries.cautions: Lofepramine is safest in overdose; dosulepin the most dangerous.

entries.mechanism: Irreversibly inhibit monoamine oxidase, raising synaptic monoamines.
entries.uses: Treatment-resistant and atypical depression.
entries.cautions: The cheese reaction — tyramine-rich foods precipitate hypertensive crisis; serotonin syndrome with SSRIs and pethidine; long washout when switching.

entries.mechanism: Reversible and selective, so tyramine can displace it — greatly reducing the dietary hazard.
entries.uses: Depression, social anxiety.
entries.cautions: Fewer dietary restrictions but still serotonergic interactions.

entries.mechanism: Vortioxetine combines reuptake inhibition with several receptor actions; agomelatine is melatonergic agonist and 5-HT2C antagonist.
entries.uses: Depression, particularly with sleep disturbance or cognitive symptoms.
entries.cautions: Agomelatine requires LFT monitoring; nausea with vortioxetine.

entries.mechanism: Rapid glutamatergic modulation producing antidepressant effect within hours rather than weeks.
entries.uses: Treatment-resistant depression, under supervised administration.
entries.cautions: Dissociation, sedation, raised BP; misuse potential; must be given in a monitored setting.

entries.mechanism: Mechanism incompletely understood — affects inositol and glycogen synthase kinase-3 signalling among others.
entries.uses: Prophylaxis in bipolar disorder; augmentation in resistant depression; reduces suicide risk.
entries.cautions: Very narrow therapeutic index requiring blood-level monitoring. Renally cleared, so dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides push it into toxicity: tremor, then ataxia, confusion, seizures. Long term affects thyroid and kidney; teratogenic (Ebstein anomaly).

entries.mechanism: Increases GABA availability and blocks voltage-gated sodium channels.
entries.uses: Bipolar disorder; generalised and focal epilepsy; migraine prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: Severely teratogenic — neural-tube defects and neurodevelopmental harm; avoided in anyone of childbearing potential unless strict conditions are met. Weight gain, tremor, hepatotoxicity, hair thinning, pancreatitis, hyperammonaemia.

entries.mechanism: Stabilises presynaptic membranes and reduces glutamate release.
entries.uses: Bipolar depression; focal and generalised epilepsy.
entries.cautions: Stevens-Johnson syndrome if titrated too fast — hence slow escalation. Valproate doubles its level. Comparatively safe in pregnancy, which is why it is favoured in women of childbearing age.

entries.mechanism: Blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the mesolimbic pathway, relieving hallucinations and delusions — but dopamine has other jobs, and blocking it elsewhere produces the side effects.
entries.uses: Schizophrenia, mania, acute agitation, delirium, intractable nausea.
entries.cautions: Prominent extrapyramidal effects — parkinsonism, acute dystonia, akathisia, and long-term tardive dyskinesia; raised prolactin; QT prolongation; neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

entries.mechanism: D2 blockade with substantial histamine, muscarinic and alpha-1 antagonism.
entries.uses: Schizophrenia; intractable hiccup; sedation in agitation.
entries.cautions: Sedation, postural hypotension, photosensitivity and skin pigmentation; lowers seizure threshold.

entries.mechanism: Esterified in oil for slow release over weeks — a formulation solution to non-adherence rather than a pharmacological one.
entries.uses: Schizophrenia where adherence is the main obstacle.
entries.cautions: Same extrapyramidal risks, but side effects cannot be stopped quickly once injected.

entries.mechanism: D2 and 5-HT2A antagonism — the serotonergic component reduces movement side effects.
entries.uses: Schizophrenia, bipolar mania and maintenance; agitation (IM).
entries.cautions: Marked weight gain, diabetes and dyslipidaemia — the metabolic trade-off for fewer movement effects.

entries.mechanism: D2 and 5-HT2A antagonism; more D2-weighted than olanzapine. Paliperidone is risperidone's active metabolite, available as long-acting injection.
entries.uses: Schizophrenia; irritability in autism; bipolar mania.
entries.cautions: Hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction); extrapyramidal effects at higher doses.

entries.mechanism: Loose D2 binding with strong H1 and 5-HT2A antagonism.
entries.uses: Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder including bipolar depression; low-dose off-label for insomnia.
entries.cautions: Sedation, postural hypotension, weight gain; minimal movement effects, hence its use in Parkinson's psychosis.

entries.mechanism: Stabilises rather than blocks dopamine transmission — dampening where dopamine is high, supporting where low.
entries.uses: Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, adjunct in depression.
entries.cautions: Akathisia is characteristic; impulse-control problems; metabolically the most favourable atypical.

entries.mechanism: Weak D2 with broad receptor activity; uniquely effective where others fail.
entries.uses: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
entries.cautions: Agranulocytosis demanding mandatory blood monitoring; myocarditis, severe constipation and ileus, seizures, hypersalivation. Levels rise sharply if the patient stops smoking.

entries.mechanism: Restores the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase, without which cerebral glucose metabolism fails.
entries.uses: Prevention and treatment of Wernicke's encephalopathy in alcohol dependence, hyperemesis and malnutrition.
entries.cautions: Must be given BEFORE any glucose load — glucose first consumes residual thiamine and can precipitate the very encephalopathy you are preventing.

entries.mechanism: Blocks the second step of alcohol metabolism so acetaldehyde accumulates, producing violent flushing, nausea and palpitations — the deterrent IS the toxicity.
entries.uses: Maintenance of abstinence in alcohol dependence, under supervision.
entries.cautions: The reaction can be severe and occasionally fatal; hidden alcohol in mouthwash and some medicines triggers it. Requires informed, motivated consent.

entries.mechanism: Restores the glutamate-GABA balance disturbed by chronic alcohol exposure, reducing craving rather than punishing drinking.
entries.uses: Maintenance of abstinence after detoxification.
entries.cautions: Diarrhoea; renally cleared; safe in liver disease, unlike disulfiram.

entries.mechanism: Partially stimulates the receptor to relieve craving while simultaneously blocking nicotine from producing its full reward — both halves of the problem at once.
entries.uses: Smoking cessation, the most effective single agent.
entries.cautions: Vivid dreams, nausea; earlier neuropsychiatric warnings largely not confirmed.

entries.mechanism: Substitutes a controlled, slowly absorbed nicotine dose without combustion products.
entries.uses: Smoking cessation.
entries.cautions: Local irritation; the tar and combustion products, not nicotine, cause most smoking-related disease.

entries.mechanism: As varenicline, from a plant alkaloid used in eastern Europe for decades — and far cheaper.
entries.uses: Smoking cessation.
entries.cautions: Nausea, sleep disturbance.

entries.mechanism: Suppresses the noradrenergic overactivity that produces most physical opioid withdrawal symptoms.
entries.uses: Symptomatic management of opioid withdrawal.
entries.cautions: Hypotension and bradycardia; does not treat craving.

entries.mechanism: Increase synaptic dopamine and noradrenaline in the prefrontal cortex, improving focus — the paradox resolves once you see these circuits are under-active in ADHD.
entries.uses: ADHD; narcolepsy.
entries.cautions: Reduced appetite and growth, insomnia, raised heart rate and blood pressure, tics; controlled drug with misuse potential.

entries.mechanism: Reverse the monoamine transporters, forcing dopamine and noradrenaline out into the synapse; lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug, which slows onset and reduces misuse.
entries.uses: ADHD; binge-eating disorder; narcolepsy.
entries.cautions: As methylphenidate, with greater cardiovascular and dependence concerns.

entries.mechanism: Raises prefrontal noradrenaline without significant dopaminergic reward — hence non-stimulant, non-controlled.
entries.uses: ADHD where stimulants are unsuitable or misuse is a concern.
entries.cautions: Slow onset over weeks; hepatotoxicity (rare); suicidal ideation warning.

entries.mechanism: Strengthens prefrontal network signalling via postsynaptic alpha-2A receptors.
entries.uses: ADHD, especially with tics or where stimulants are poorly tolerated.
entries.cautions: Sedation, hypotension, bradycardia; rebound hypertension on abrupt stopping.

entries.mechanism: Weak dopamine reuptake inhibition with orexinergic and histaminergic effects.
entries.uses: Narcolepsy; obstructive sleep apnoea with residual sleepiness.
entries.cautions: Headache, anxiety; serious skin reactions; reduces contraceptive efficacy by enzyme induction.

entries.mechanism: Increases histaminergic wakefulness from the tuberomammillary nucleus — the mirror image of the orexin antagonists.
entries.uses: Narcolepsy with or without cataplexy.
entries.cautions: Insomnia, headache; QT prolongation; not a controlled drug, unlike its alternatives.

entries.mechanism: Consolidates slow-wave sleep, reducing cataplexy and daytime sleepiness.
entries.uses: Narcolepsy with cataplexy.
entries.cautions: Profound CNS and respiratory depression with alcohol; high abuse potential; strictly controlled distribution.

entries.mechanism: Binds synaptic vesicle protein 2A, modulating neurotransmitter release — a mechanism unlike the others.
entries.uses: Focal and generalised epilepsy; status epilepticus; often first-line in pregnancy.
entries.cautions: Mood and behaviour change — irritability, aggression, low mood — the main reason for stopping. Few interactions, renally cleared.

entries.mechanism: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, reducing rapid repetitive firing.
entries.uses: Focal epilepsy; trigeminal neuralgia; bipolar disorder.
entries.cautions: A powerful enzyme inducer causing contraceptive failure. Hyponatraemia (SIADH); serious skin reactions — screen HLA-B*15:02 in Han Chinese, Thai and other Southeast Asian ancestries, where the risk is many times higher; it induces its own metabolism.

entries.mechanism: Carbamazepine analogues with less autoinduction and fewer interactions.
entries.uses: Focal epilepsy.
entries.cautions: More hyponatraemia than carbamazepine; cross-reactive skin hypersensitivity.

entries.mechanism: Blocks sodium channels; displays zero-order (saturable) kinetics.
entries.uses: Status epilepticus; focal and tonic-clonic seizures.
entries.cautions: Small dose changes cause large level changes — the textbook narrow-therapeutic-index drug. Ataxia, nystagmus, gum hypertrophy, hirsutism, coarse facies, cerebellar atrophy; strong enzyme inducer; purple glove syndrome on IV use.

entries.mechanism: Sodium-channel blockade, GABA enhancement, AMPA/kainate antagonism and carbonic anhydrase inhibition.
entries.uses: Focal and generalised epilepsy; migraine prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: Cognitive slowing and word-finding difficulty, paraesthesia, weight loss, renal stones, acute glaucoma; teratogenic.

entries.mechanism: Binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing excitatory neurotransmitter release. Despite the name it does not act on GABA receptors at all.
entries.uses: Neuropathic pain; focal epilepsy; restless legs.
entries.cautions: Sedation, dizziness, weight gain, oedema; saturable absorption means dose increases give diminishing levels. Genuine misuse potential and respiratory depression with opioids; now a controlled drug in the UK.

entries.mechanism: As gabapentin, with linear and more predictable absorption.
entries.uses: Neuropathic pain; generalised anxiety disorder; focal epilepsy; fibromyalgia.
entries.cautions: Same profile; more reinforcing than gabapentin and more often misused; renally cleared, so it accumulates and sedates heavily in kidney impairment.

entries.mechanism: Blocks thalamic T-type calcium currents that generate the 3-Hz spike-wave discharge.
entries.uses: Absence seizures — first-line.
entries.cautions: GI upset, hiccups; ineffective for other seizure types.

entries.mechanism: Lacosamide enhances slow inactivation of sodium channels rather than fast inactivation.
entries.uses: Focal epilepsy, adjunct or monotherapy.
entries.cautions: Dizziness, diplopia; PR prolongation with lacosamide; zonisamide causes weight loss and stones.

entries.mechanism: Perampanel blocks AMPA glutamate receptors; brivaracetam is a higher-affinity SV2A ligand.
entries.uses: Focal and generalised epilepsy.
entries.cautions: Perampanel causes serious aggression and psychiatric effects.

entries.mechanism: Irreversibly blocks GABA breakdown, raising brain GABA.
entries.uses: Infantile spasms (first-line with West syndrome and tuberous sclerosis); refractory focal epilepsy.
entries.cautions: Irreversible concentric visual field loss in a third of patients — an accepted trade only because infantile spasms are so damaging.

entries.mechanism: Multiple non-CB1 mechanisms; exact antiseizure action unclear.
entries.uses: Dravet, Lennox-Gastaut and tuberous sclerosis-related seizures.
entries.cautions: Hepatotoxicity, especially with valproate; raises clobazam levels.

entries.class: Dopamine precursor with peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor
entries.mechanism: Dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier but levodopa can, and is converted to dopamine within the brain. The decarboxylase inhibitor blocks that conversion peripherally, so more reaches the brain and nausea is reduced.
entries.uses: Parkinson's disease — the most effective symptomatic treatment.
entries.cautions: Nausea, postural hypotension, hallucinations; after years, motor fluctuations, wearing off and dyskinesias — the central long-term challenge.

entries.mechanism: Directly stimulate dopamine receptors, bypassing the need for surviving neurons.
entries.uses: Parkinson's disease, especially in younger patients; restless legs syndrome.
entries.cautions: Notorious impulse-control disorders — gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping — which must be asked about directly; sudden-onset sleep; hallucinations.

entries.mechanism: Slow the breakdown of dopamine within the brain, extending what dopamine remains.
entries.uses: Early Parkinson's; adjunct to levodopa.
entries.cautions: Insomnia; serotonin syndrome with antidepressants; selegiline metabolises to amfetamine derivatives.

entries.mechanism: Block peripheral catechol-O-methyltransferase, prolonging levodopa's half-life.
entries.uses: Levodopa wearing off.
entries.cautions: Enhances dyskinesia; orange discolouration of urine; diarrhoea.

entries.mechanism: Enhances dopamine release and blocks NMDA receptors.
entries.uses: Levodopa-induced dyskinesia; fatigue in multiple sclerosis.
entries.cautions: Livedo reticularis, ankle oedema, confusion.

entries.mechanism: Restore the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the striatum by blocking the cholinergic side — which is why they work for drug-induced parkinsonism.
entries.uses: Drug-induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia from antipsychotics; tremor-predominant Parkinson's.
entries.cautions: They treat parkinsonism and acute dystonia but do NOT help tardive dyskinesia and may worsen it. Full anticholinergic burden; confusion in the elderly; misused for euphoria.

entries.mechanism: Antihistamine-derived muscarinic blockade with NMDA antagonism; sold as a “muscle relaxant” though it has no action on muscle or the neuromuscular junction at all.
entries.uses: Drug-induced parkinsonism; musculoskeletal pain with spasm.
entries.cautions: Anticholinergic burden; euphoriant and misused; dangerous in overdose with cardiotoxicity and seizures at modest multiples of the therapeutic dose.

entries.mechanism: Deplete presynaptic dopamine stores.
entries.uses: Chorea in Huntington's disease; tardive dyskinesia.
entries.cautions: Depression and suicidality (tetrabenazine); parkinsonism.

entries.mechanism: Cleaves SNARE proteins so acetylcholine vesicles cannot fuse with the terminal membrane — chemical denervation lasting three to four months until new terminals sprout.
entries.uses: Focal spasticity and dystonia; chronic migraine; hyperhidrosis; overactive bladder; cosmetic use.
entries.cautions: Distant spread causes dysphagia and respiratory weakness; effect is temporary by design and there is no practical antidote.

entries.mechanism: Activates presynaptic GABA-B receptors in the spinal cord, reducing excitatory drive onto motor neurons.
entries.uses: Spasticity in multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury and cerebral palsy; intrathecal for severe cases.
entries.cautions: Sedation and weakness — reducing tone can remove support a patient uses to stand. Abrupt withdrawal, especially intrathecal, causes life-threatening fever, rigidity and seizures.

entries.mechanism: Reduces spinal excitatory transmitter release via alpha-2 receptors.
entries.uses: Spasticity.
entries.cautions: Sedation, hypotension, hepatotoxicity; levels raised enormously by ciprofloxacin (CYP1A2 inhibition).

entries.mechanism: Structurally a tricyclic; acts on brainstem descending pathways, not on muscle. Its antimuscarinic and sedative effects come from the tricyclic scaffold.
entries.uses: Acute musculoskeletal pain with spasm, short courses.
entries.cautions: Sedation, dry mouth, confusion in the elderly; serotonin syndrome with SSRIs and MAOIs; no benefit beyond two weeks.

entries.mechanism: Central depressant action; mechanism poorly defined and probably largely sedative.
entries.uses: Acute musculoskeletal spasm.
entries.cautions: Sedation, dizziness; urine may turn brown-black.

entries.mechanism: Reduces presynaptic glutamate release and blocks persistent sodium currents, limiting excitotoxicity.
entries.uses: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis — it extends survival by months rather than halting decline.
entries.cautions: Nausea, asthenia, deranged LFTs requiring monitoring.

entries.mechanism: Raises brain acetylcholine on the basis that cholinergic neurons are lost early in Alzheimer's.
entries.uses: Mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease.
entries.cautions: Nausea, diarrhoea, bradycardia and syncope, vivid dreams; modest symptomatic benefit only.

entries.mechanism: As donepezil; rivastigmine also inhibits butyrylcholinesterase and comes as a patch.
entries.uses: Alzheimer's; rivastigmine also for Parkinson's disease dementia and Lewy body dementia.
entries.cautions: Same cholinergic profile; patch reduces GI effects.

entries.mechanism: Dampens excess glutamatergic signalling and the excitotoxicity it causes.
entries.uses: Moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease.
entries.cautions: Dizziness, headache, confusion; generally well tolerated.

entries.mechanism: Bind and promote clearance of amyloid-beta — the first plausibly disease-modifying agents in Alzheimer's.
entries.uses: Early Alzheimer's with confirmed amyloid pathology.
entries.cautions: Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) — brain oedema and microhaemorrhage requiring MRI monitoring; APOE4 homozygotes at highest risk.

entries.mechanism: Shifts the cytokine balance away from pro-inflammatory Th1 responses and reduces lymphocyte trafficking across the blood-brain barrier.
entries.uses: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.
entries.cautions: Flu-like reactions after each injection, injection-site necrosis, deranged LFTs, neutralising antibodies reducing efficacy over time.

entries.mechanism: A synthetic mixture resembling myelin basic protein that acts as a decoy antigen, diverting the autoimmune response.
entries.uses: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.
entries.cautions: Injection-site lipoatrophy; a transient post-injection flushing and chest-tightness reaction that alarms patients.

entries.mechanism: Trap lymphocytes inside lymph nodes by removing the S1P signal they need to exit — they never reach the CNS.
entries.uses: Relapsing multiple sclerosis; ozanimod also in ulcerative colitis.
entries.cautions: First-dose bradycardia requiring monitoring; macular oedema; varicella reactivation — check immunity first.

entries.mechanism: Dimethyl fumarate activates the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway; teriflunomide blocks pyrimidine synthesis in proliferating lymphocytes.
entries.uses: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.
entries.cautions: Flushing and GI upset (fumarate); lymphopenia and PML; teriflunomide is teratogenic with a very long half-life needing cholestyramine washout.

entries.mechanism: Selectively depletes lymphocytes; given as short courses a year apart with lasting effect.
entries.uses: Highly active relapsing multiple sclerosis.
entries.cautions: Lymphopenia, herpes zoster, malignancy signal.

entries.mechanism: Natalizumab blocks alpha-4 integrin so lymphocytes cannot cross the blood-brain barrier; ocrelizumab depletes CD20 B-cells.
entries.uses: Relapsing-remitting and primary progressive multiple sclerosis.
entries.cautions: Natalizumab risks progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy — stratified by JC virus antibody status.

entries.class: H3 antagonist and weak H1 agonist
entries.mechanism: Increases cochlear and vestibular blood flow and modulates vestibular nucleus activity.
entries.uses: Ménière's disease; recurrent vertigo.
entries.cautions: Dyspepsia, headache; caution in asthma and peptic ulcer.

entries.mechanism: Raise acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, compensating for antibody-depleted receptors.
entries.uses: Myasthenia gravis.
entries.cautions: Cholinergic crisis from excess dosing closely mimics myasthenic crisis — the key clinical distinction.

entries.mechanism: Multiple immunomodulatory actions including antibody neutralisation and Fc receptor blockade.
entries.uses: Guillain-Barré syndrome; CIDP; myasthenic crisis.
entries.cautions: Thrombosis, renal impairment and aseptic meningitis at high dose; infusion reactions.

entries.mechanism: Lipophilic enough to reach cerebral vessels, reducing vasospasm-related ischaemia.
entries.uses: Prevention of delayed cerebral ischaemia after subarachnoid haemorrhage.
entries.cautions: Hypotension; must be given orally or by central line — peripheral IV causes severe phlebitis.

entries.mechanism: Binds penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) that cross-link peptidoglycan, so the cell wall fails and the bacterium bursts. Humans have no cell wall — excellent selective toxicity. Bactericidal.
entries.uses: Chest, ear, dental and urinary infection; H. pylori eradication; endocarditis prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: Allergy from mild rash to anaphylaxis — always ask; GI upset; destroyed by beta-lactamases. Rash if given in glandular fever.

entries.mechanism: Clavulanic acid irreversibly inhibits beta-lactamase, rescuing the penicillin from destruction.
entries.uses: Resistant respiratory, urinary, bite and intra-abdominal infection; sinusitis.
entries.cautions: Cholestatic hepatitis, which may appear weeks after the course; C. difficile risk; diarrhoea.

entries.mechanism: A bulky side chain shields the beta-lactam ring from staphylococcal penicillinase. Narrow spectrum.
entries.uses: Staphylococcal skin and soft-tissue infection, osteomyelitis, endocarditis.
entries.cautions: Cholestatic jaundice, sometimes delayed; poor oral absorption — take on an empty stomach.

entries.mechanism: As amoxicillin; narrow spectrum focused on streptococci, meningococci and syphilis.
entries.uses: Serious streptococcal infection, meningitis, endocarditis, syphilis.
entries.cautions: Acid-labile so not oral; high doses deliver a significant potassium load.

entries.mechanism: Acid-stable version of benzylpenicillin.
entries.uses: Streptococcal pharyngitis; dental abscess; splenectomy prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: Narrow spectrum; must be taken on an empty stomach.

entries.mechanism: Poorly soluble salts release penicillin slowly from the injection site for days to weeks.
entries.uses: Syphilis; rheumatic fever prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: Painful injection; never give intravenously — the suspension embolises.

entries.mechanism: As amoxicillin; the standard parenteral aminopenicillin.
entries.uses: Neonatal sepsis (with gentamicin); Listeria meningitis; enterococcal infection.
entries.cautions: Rash; poor oral bioavailability compared with amoxicillin.

entries.mechanism: Broad beta-lactam activity including Pseudomonas, protected by tazobactam.
entries.uses: Hospital-acquired and neutropenic sepsis; intra-abdominal infection; necrotising fasciitis.
entries.cautions: C. difficile; broad-spectrum pressure on flora; sodium load.

entries.mechanism: Beta-lactam with the same wall target as penicillins.
entries.uses: Skin and soft-tissue infection; urinary infection; option in mild penicillin allergy.
entries.cautions: About 10% cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy; C. difficile risk.

entries.mechanism: As cefalexin; excellent staphylococcal cover.
entries.uses: Surgical prophylaxis — the default agent worldwide.
entries.cautions: Same class cautions; requires redosing in long operations.

entries.mechanism: Extended Gram-negative cover over first-generation agents.
entries.uses: Surgical prophylaxis; respiratory and urinary infection.
entries.cautions: C. difficile risk; poorer CSF penetration than third-generation agents.

entries.mechanism: Broad Gram-negative cover with good CSF penetration; ceftriaxone is once-daily.
entries.uses: Meningitis, severe pneumonia, gonorrhoea, pyelonephritis, enteric fever — workhorses for serious infection.
entries.cautions: Biliary sludging; ceftriaxone must not be given with calcium-containing fluids in neonates; C. difficile.

entries.mechanism: Oral agents with useful Gram-negative activity.
entries.uses: Otitis media, urinary infection, gonorrhoea (cefixime).
entries.cautions: Diarrhoea; resistance selection; cefdinir turns stools red with iron.

entries.mechanism: Extended Gram-negative spectrum including Pseudomonas.
entries.uses: Hospital-acquired infection, febrile neutropenia, endophthalmitis.
entries.cautions: Neurotoxicity in renal impairment; ceftazidime has weak Gram-positive cover.

entries.mechanism: Binds PBP2a, the altered protein that makes MRSA resistant to other beta-lactams.
entries.uses: MRSA skin infection and pneumonia.
entries.cautions: The only beta-lactam with reliable MRSA activity.

entries.mechanism: Extremely broad beta-lactam activity, stable to most beta-lactamases — the reserve agents.
entries.uses: Severe or multi-resistant infection; ESBL producers; neonatal meningitis.
entries.cautions: Seizures (imipenem more so); reduces valproate levels dramatically; stewardship restricted. Cilastatin blocks renal dehydropeptidase, protecting imipenem rather than acting on bacteria.

entries.mechanism: Beta-lactam active only against aerobic Gram-negatives; no cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy.
entries.uses: Gram-negative infection in severe beta-lactam allergy.
entries.cautions: Narrow spectrum limits empirical use.

entries.mechanism: Novel beta-lactamase inhibitors restore activity against carbapenem-resistant organisms; cefiderocol is a siderophore cephalosporin that hijacks bacterial iron transport to get inside.
entries.uses: Carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative infection.
entries.cautions: Last-line agents under strict stewardship; resistance already emerging.

entries.mechanism: Binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors, blocking cross-linking by a mechanism entirely different from the beta-lactams.
entries.uses: MRSA bacteraemia and severe Gram-positive infection (IV); oral for C. difficile colitis.
entries.cautions: Nephrotoxic; requires level monitoring; “red man syndrome” from rapid infusion is histamine release, not allergy. Poor oral absorption is turned to advantage — staying in the bowel is exactly what you want for C. difficile.

entries.mechanism: As vancomycin, with a long half-life allowing once-daily dosing.
entries.uses: Gram-positive infection; outpatient parenteral therapy.
entries.cautions: Less nephrotoxic; still monitored.

entries.mechanism: Inserts into the Gram-positive membrane and depolarises it.
entries.uses: MRSA bacteraemia, right-sided endocarditis, skin infection.
entries.cautions: Inactivated by pulmonary surfactant — useless in pneumonia; raises creatine kinase.

entries.mechanism: Disrupt the Gram-negative outer membrane like a detergent.
entries.uses: Last-line therapy for multi-resistant Gram-negatives.
entries.cautions: Nephrotoxic and neurotoxic — revived only because of resistance.

entries.mechanism: Blocks MurA, the very first committed step of peptidoglycan synthesis — upstream of every other cell-wall agent.
entries.uses: Uncomplicated UTI (single oral dose); multi-resistant infection (IV).
entries.cautions: Resistance develops rapidly if used as monotherapy systemically.

entries.mechanism: Bacitracin blocks cell-wall lipid carrier recycling; mupirocin inhibits bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase.
entries.uses: Impetigo; nasal MRSA decolonisation (mupirocin).
entries.cautions: Too nephrotoxic for systemic use; mupirocin resistance follows widespread use.

entries.mechanism: Binds the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, blocking translocation. Long tissue half-life allows short courses.
entries.uses: Atypical pneumonia, chlamydia, gonorrhoea (combination), cholera, trachoma, enteric fever.
entries.cautions: QT prolongation; GI upset; cardiovascular mortality signal; drives macrolide resistance.

entries.mechanism: As azithromycin; erythromycin additionally stimulates motilin receptors, which is why it doubles as a prokinetic.
entries.uses: Respiratory and skin infection; penicillin allergy; H. pylori eradication; gastroparesis (erythromycin).
entries.cautions: Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors — the warfarin and statin interactions live here. QT prolongation; cholestatic hepatitis.

entries.mechanism: Binds the 30S subunit, blocking tRNA docking. Bacteriostatic, broad-spectrum.
entries.uses: Atypical and respiratory infection, acne, chlamydia, Lyme disease, cholera, malaria prophylaxis, rickettsial and scrub typhus infection.
entries.cautions: Avoid in pregnancy and children under 12 — it binds calcium in developing teeth and bone. Photosensitivity; oesophageal ulceration — take with water sitting up; absorption reduced by calcium, iron and antacids.

entries.mechanism: As doxycycline.
entries.uses: Acne; rosacea; ophthalmic ointment for trachoma.
entries.cautions: Minocycline causes skin pigmentation, vestibular effects and drug-induced lupus.

entries.mechanism: Binds the 30S subunit causing mistranslation; uptake requires oxygen, so it fails against anaerobes. Bactericidal and concentration-dependent.
entries.uses: Serious Gram-negative sepsis; synergy in endocarditis; neonatal sepsis.
entries.cautions: Narrow therapeutic index — nephrotoxicity and irreversible ototoxicity; levels monitored. Not absorbed orally. Avoid in pregnancy and myasthenia gravis.

entries.mechanism: As gentamicin; amikacin resists many inactivating enzymes.
entries.uses: Resistant Gram-negative infection; MDR-TB; nebulised tobramycin in cystic fibrosis.
entries.cautions: Same toxicity profile.

entries.mechanism: As gentamicin; the first effective antituberculous drug.
entries.uses: Tuberculosis (second-line); plague; tularaemia; brucellosis.
entries.cautions: Vestibular toxicity predominates over cochlear; intramuscular only.

entries.mechanism: Binds the 50S subunit; suppresses bacterial toxin production, which is why it is added in toxic shock.
entries.uses: Anaerobic infection, severe skin and soft-tissue infection, necrotising fasciitis, bone and joint infection.
entries.cautions: The classic C. difficile precursor; diarrhoea.

entries.mechanism: Bind the 50S subunit preventing initiation complex formation; excellent oral bioavailability.
entries.uses: MRSA and VRE infection; MDR-TB.
entries.cautions: Reversible myelosuppression; peripheral and optic neuropathy beyond 28 days; a weak MAOI — serotonin syndrome with SSRIs.

entries.mechanism: Binds the 50S subunit blocking peptidyl transferase.
entries.uses: Bacterial conjunctivitis (topical); epidemic meningitis where alternatives are unavailable.
entries.cautions: Systemically — aplastic anaemia and grey baby syndrome; topical use is safe.

entries.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial elongation factor G.
entries.uses: Staphylococcal skin and eye infection; adjunct in bone infection.
entries.cautions: Rapid resistance if used alone systemically.

entries.mechanism: As gentamicin, but far too nephrotoxic and ototoxic for systemic use — so it is confined to surfaces and the gut lumen, where it is not absorbed.
entries.uses: Topical ear, eye and skin combinations; bowel decontamination before surgery; hepatic encephalopathy (historic).
entries.cautions: Contact sensitisation is common with topical use; ototoxicity if applied to a perforated tympanic membrane or absorbed through broken skin.

entries.mechanism: Binds the 30S subunit; narrow spectrum.
entries.uses: Gonorrhoea where cephalosporins cannot be used.
entries.cautions: Intramuscular only; ineffective for pharyngeal infection.

entries.mechanism: Inhibits DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, preventing DNA supercoiling and replication. Bactericidal with excellent tissue penetration.
entries.uses: Urinary, gastrointestinal and Pseudomonas infection; enteric fever; prostatitis.
entries.cautions: Tendon damage and rupture (worse with steroids and in the elderly); QT prolongation; C. difficile; lowered seizure threshold; aortic aneurysm signal. Absorption blocked by calcium and iron; inhibits CYP1A2 raising theophylline and tizanidine levels.

entries.mechanism: As ciprofloxacin with better Gram-positive and atypical cover.
entries.uses: Severe community-acquired pneumonia; MDR- TB; ophthalmic drops.
entries.cautions: Same class warnings; moxifloxacin has the greatest QT effect and poor urinary penetration.

entries.mechanism: Reduced by anaerobic organisms into reactive intermediates that fragment microbial DNA — selectivity comes from requiring an anaerobic environment.
entries.uses: Anaerobic and dental infection, intra-abdominal sepsis, C. difficile, bacterial vaginosis, giardiasis, amoebiasis, trichomoniasis.
entries.cautions: Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol — severe flushing and vomiting from acetaldehyde build-up; metallic taste; peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use.

entries.mechanism: As metronidazole with a longer half-life allowing single-dose therapy.
entries.uses: Giardiasis, amoebiasis, trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis.
entries.cautions: Same alcohol interaction.

entries.mechanism: Blocks bacterial folate synthesis; bacteria must synthesise folate while we absorb it — the basis of selectivity.
entries.uses: Uncomplicated urinary tract infection.
entries.cautions: Raises potassium and creatinine (blocks tubular secretion); folate antagonist — avoid in first trimester; interacts with methotrexate.

entries.mechanism: Blocks two consecutive steps in folate synthesis, giving synergy.
entries.uses: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia treatment and prophylaxis; nocardia; melioidosis; toxoplasmosis; some resistant UTIs.
entries.cautions: Severe skin reactions, marrow suppression, hyperkalaemia, renal impairment; sulfonamide allergy.

entries.mechanism: Reduced by bacterial nitroreductases into reactive species damaging ribosomes and DNA; concentrates in urine, which is exactly where it is needed.
entries.uses: Uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection.
entries.cautions: Ineffective if eGFR is low — it cannot reach therapeutic urinary concentration; pulmonary fibrosis and hepatitis with long-term use; avoid at term and in G6PD deficiency.

entries.mechanism: Binds bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, blocking transcription.
entries.uses: Tuberculosis; leprosy; staphylococcal prosthetic infection; meningococcal prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: The archetypal enzyme inducer — it wrecks the contraceptive pill and lowers levels of countless drugs; turns urine, tears and contact lenses orange; hepatitis. Never used alone.

entries.mechanism: Hydrolysed in acidic urine to formaldehyde, which is non-specifically bactericidal — so resistance essentially cannot develop.
entries.uses: Recurrent UTI prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: Requires acidic urine; ineffective for active upper tract infection.

entries.mechanism: Prodrug activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase; blocks mycolic acid synthesis in the cell wall.
entries.uses: Tuberculosis — the I of RIPE; latent TB treatment.
entries.cautions: Peripheral neuropathy — prevented by co-prescribing pyridoxine (vitamin B6); hepatitis; drug-induced lupus. Acetylation status varies genetically.

entries.mechanism: Blocks bacterial transcription; sterilises semi-dormant organisms.
entries.uses: Tuberculosis, all phases.
entries.cautions: Enzyme induction wrecks concomitant therapy — a particular problem with antiretrovirals; orange secretions; hepatitis.

entries.mechanism: Active in the acidic environment inside macrophages, killing semi-dormant organisms other drugs miss.
entries.uses: Tuberculosis — intensive phase.
entries.cautions: Hepatotoxicity; hyperuricaemia and gout; arthralgia.

entries.mechanism: Blocks arabinogalactan synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall.
entries.uses: Tuberculosis — intensive phase.
entries.cautions: Optic neuritis with loss of colour vision — baseline and monitored visual acuity; dose-reduce in renal impairment.

entries.mechanism: As rifampicin; rifapentine's long half-life allows weekly dosing, rifabutin induces enzymes less.
entries.uses: Latent TB (rifapentine with isoniazid); TB in patients on antiretrovirals (rifabutin).
entries.cautions: Rifabutin causes uveitis and neutropenia.

entries.mechanism: Blocks the proton pump of mycobacterial ATP synthase — a target unique to the organism, and the first genuinely new TB mechanism in forty years.
entries.uses: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
entries.cautions: QT prolongation; very long terminal half-life (months); hepatotoxicity.

entries.mechanism: Block mycolic acid synthesis and generate reactive nitrogen species under anaerobic conditions.
entries.uses: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, in combination regimens.
entries.cautions: QT prolongation; pretomanid used only within defined regimens.

entries.mechanism: Block cell-wall D-alanine incorporation.
entries.uses: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
entries.cautions: Prominent neuropsychiatric toxicity — psychosis, depression, seizures.

entries.mechanism: Isoniazid-related inhibition of mycolic acid synthesis.
entries.uses: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
entries.cautions: Severe GI intolerance; hypothyroidism; hepatotoxicity.

entries.mechanism: Binds mycobacterial DNA and generates reactive oxygen species; also anti-inflammatory.
entries.uses: Leprosy (multidrug therapy); multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
entries.cautions: Red-brown skin discolouration that persists for months — a major reason for non-adherence and stigma; QT prolongation.

entries.mechanism: Blocks dihydropteroate synthase.
entries.uses: Leprosy; dermatitis herpetiformis; PCP prophylaxis.
entries.cautions: Haemolysis, especially in G6PD deficiency; methaemoglobinaemia; dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome.

entries.mechanism: Competes with para-aminobenzoic acid in mycobacterial folate synthesis.
entries.uses: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, later-line.
entries.cautions: Severe GI intolerance; hypothyroidism.

entries.mechanism: Inhibits fungal CYP51 (lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase), blocking ergosterol synthesis. Selectivity leans on ergosterol being fungal-specific.
entries.uses: Candidiasis — oral, oesophageal, vaginal and systemic; cryptococcal meningitis.
entries.cautions: Potent CYP2C9/3A4 inhibitor — raises warfarin, statin and phenytoin levels; hepatotoxicity; QT prolongation; teratogenic at high dose.

entries.mechanism: As fluconazole with broader mould activity.
entries.uses: Aspergillosis; talaromycosis (Penicillium marneffei); histoplasmosis; prophylaxis in haematology.
entries.cautions: Heavy CYP3A4 interactions; voriconazole causes visual disturbance, photosensitivity and skin cancer with long use; itraconazole is negatively inotropic.

entries.mechanism: Ergosterol synthesis inhibition applied locally.
entries.uses: Vaginal and cutaneous candidiasis; seborrhoeic dermatitis; tinea.
entries.cautions: Local irritation; even vaginal miconazole can raise INR on warfarin.

entries.mechanism: Binds ergosterol and punches pores in the fungal membrane; not absorbed from the gut, so it stays exactly where applied.
entries.uses: Oral and gastrointestinal candidiasis; vaginal candidiasis.
entries.cautions: Local only; ineffective for systemic infection by design.

entries.mechanism: Binds ergosterol forming membrane pores; liposomal formulation reduces toxicity substantially.
entries.uses: Severe systemic fungal infection; cryptococcal meningitis; visceral leishmaniasis; mucormycosis.
entries.cautions: Nicknamed “ampho-terrible” — nephrotoxicity, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, infusion rigors. A reminder of how hard it is to poison a fungus without harming the host.

entries.mechanism: Taken up by fungal cytosine permease (which human cells lack) and converted to 5-fluorouracil inside the fungus, blocking DNA synthesis.
entries.uses: Cryptococcal meningitis, always with amphotericin — resistance is rapid if used alone.
entries.cautions: Marrow suppression and hepatotoxicity requiring level monitoring; the human gut flora can convert it to 5-FU.

entries.mechanism: Inhibits squalene epoxidase earlier in the ergosterol pathway; accumulates in keratin.
entries.uses: Dermatophyte nail and skin infection.
entries.cautions: Hepatotoxicity, taste disturbance (sometimes prolonged), rash; needs months for nails.

entries.mechanism: Inhibit beta-1,3-glucan synthesis in the fungal cell wall — a structure humans entirely lack, giving excellent selectivity.
entries.uses: Invasive candidiasis; salvage therapy in aspergillosis.
entries.cautions: Well tolerated; few interactions; intravenous only; poor CNS and urinary penetration.

entries.mechanism: Binds fungal microtubules, disrupting mitosis; deposits in keratin.
entries.uses: Tinea capitis in children.
entries.cautions: Enzyme inducer; teratogenic; superseded by terbinafine in adults.

entries.mechanism: Binds ergosterol in the corneal surface.
entries.uses: Fungal keratitis — the only licensed topical option in many countries.
entries.cautions: Poor penetration beyond superficial cornea.

entries.mechanism: Selenium sulfide is cytostatic to Malassezia; ciclopirox chelates metal cations essential to fungal enzymes.
entries.uses: Pityriasis versicolor; seborrhoeic dermatitis; onychomycosis (ciclopirox lacquer).
entries.cautions: Local irritation; hair discolouration with selenium.

entries.mechanism: A prodrug phosphorylated only inside infected cells by the viral thymidine kinase, then incorporated to terminate viral DNA chains — a worked example of selective toxicity.
entries.uses: Herpes simplex, varicella zoster, herpes encephalitis.
entries.cautions: Crystal nephropathy if not hydrated when given IV; neurotoxicity in renal impairment.

entries.mechanism: Better oral bioavailability than aciclovir, converted after absorption.
entries.uses: Herpes zoster and recurrent genital herpes.
entries.cautions: As aciclovir.

entries.mechanism: Active against cytomegalovirus, phosphorylated by the viral UL97 kinase.
entries.uses: CMV retinitis and disease in transplant and HIV.
entries.cautions: Marked myelosuppression; carcinogenic and teratogenic — handling precautions.

entries.mechanism: Block influenza neuraminidase so newly formed virions cannot be released from the host cell.
entries.uses: Influenza treatment and prophylaxis, most useful within 48 hours.
entries.cautions: Nausea and vomiting; modest benefit — shortens illness by about a day in otherwise healthy people.

entries.mechanism: Chain-terminates viral DNA synthesis by reverse transcriptase.
entries.uses: HIV treatment and pre-exposure prophylaxis; chronic hepatitis B.
entries.cautions: Disoproxil causes renal tubular damage and bone loss; alafenamide reduces this.

entries.mechanism: Chain termination after intracellular phosphorylation.
entries.uses: HIV combination therapy; hepatitis B.
entries.cautions: Well tolerated; hepatitis B flares if stopped abruptly; resistance emerges fast as monotherapy.

entries.mechanism: The first antiretroviral — chain-terminates reverse transcription.
entries.uses: HIV, now mainly in prevention of mother-to-child transmission.
entries.cautions: Anaemia and neutropenia; myopathy; lipoatrophy; lactic acidosis from mitochondrial toxicity.

entries.mechanism: Chain termination; no renal dose adjustment needed.
entries.uses: HIV combination therapy.
entries.cautions: Potentially fatal hypersensitivity in HLA-B*57:01 carriers — mandatory testing before use, one of pharmacogenomics' clearest wins.

entries.mechanism: Bind allosterically to reverse transcriptase, distorting its active site — they need no phosphorylation.
entries.uses: HIV combination therapy.
entries.cautions: Efavirenz: vivid dreams, dysphoria, neuropsychiatric effects. Nevirapine: severe rash and hepatitis, risk tied to CD4 count at initiation.

entries.mechanism: Prevent integration of viral DNA into the host genome.
entries.uses: First-line backbone of HIV antiretroviral therapy.
entries.cautions: Weight gain; insomnia; dolutegravir raises metformin levels.

entries.mechanism: Inhibits HIV protease; more importantly, potent CYP3A4 inhibition is exploited deliberately to boost other drugs' levels.
entries.uses: HIV combination therapy; booster in nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for COVID-19.
entries.cautions: The interaction profile is its defining feature — an enormous list of contraindicated co-prescriptions.

entries.mechanism: Block the protease that cleaves viral polyprotein into functional units, so virions assemble but remain immature and non-infectious.
entries.uses: HIV, usually ritonavir-boosted, in second-line regimens.
entries.cautions: Dyslipidaemia, lipodystrophy, GI upset; atazanavir causes benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and jaundice.

entries.mechanism: Inhibits hepatitis B polymerase at three steps; high barrier to resistance.
entries.uses: Chronic hepatitis B.
entries.cautions: Lactic acidosis; flares on discontinuation; resistance if previously lamivudine-exposed.

entries.drug: Sofosbuvir-based combinations (with velpatasvir, daclatasvir or ledipasvir)
entries.mechanism: Inhibit the hepatitis C NS5B polymerase and NS5A protein, stopping replication outright.
entries.uses: Hepatitis C — curative in the great majority, one of modern pharmacology's genuine triumphs.
entries.cautions: Reactivation of hepatitis B — screen first; interactions via P-glycoprotein; amiodarone causes severe bradycardia.

entries.mechanism: NS3/4A protease and NS5A inhibition.
entries.uses: Hepatitis C, including in renal failure.
entries.cautions: As above; contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis.

entries.mechanism: Multiple actions including lethal mutagenesis of viral RNA.
entries.uses: Hepatitis C (adjunct); viral haemorrhagic fevers; RSV (nebulised).
entries.cautions: Dose-limiting haemolytic anaemia; strongly teratogenic with prolonged washout for both partners.

entries.mechanism: Remdesivir is a nucleotide analogue inhibiting RNA polymerase; nirmatrelvir inhibits the viral main protease, boosted by ritonavir.
entries.uses: COVID-19 in those at risk of severe disease.
entries.cautions: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir has extensive CYP3A4 interactions requiring full medication review before prescribing.

entries.mechanism: Artemisinin generates free radicals within the parasite; the partner drug clears residual organisms and protects against resistance.
entries.uses: Uncomplicated falciparum malaria — the global mainstay.
entries.cautions: Must be taken with fatty food for absorption; QT prolongation.

entries.mechanism: Rapid parasite killing across the life cycle.
entries.uses: Severe falciparum malaria — superior to quinine, and the single biggest advance in malaria mortality.
entries.cautions: Delayed post-artesunate haemolysis; monitor for weeks afterwards.

entries.mechanism: As artemether-lumefantrine with different partner drugs.
entries.uses: Uncomplicated falciparum malaria; regional choice depends on resistance.
entries.cautions: Piperaquine prolongs QT; mefloquine causes neuropsychiatric effects.

entries.mechanism: Accumulates in the parasite food vacuole preventing haem detoxification.
entries.uses: Plasmodium vivax malaria where sensitive; prophylaxis in vivax areas.
entries.cautions: Widespread falciparum resistance; retinopathy with cumulative dosing; fatal in small overdose in children.

entries.mechanism: Raises lysosomal pH, impairing antigen processing and toll-like receptor signalling.
entries.uses: Systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's.
entries.cautions: Retinal toxicity with cumulative dose — annual screening after five years; QT prolongation.

entries.mechanism: Interferes with parasite haem detoxification; the oldest antimalarial.
entries.uses: Severe malaria where artesunate is unavailable; nocturnal leg cramps (discouraged).
entries.cautions: Cinchonism — tinnitus, deafness, visual disturbance; hypoglycaemia from insulin release; thrombocytopenia.

entries.mechanism: Kill dormant liver hypnozoites, preventing relapse of vivax and ovale malaria — the only agents that do.
entries.uses: Radical cure of relapsing malaria; transmission blocking.
entries.cautions: Severe haemolysis in G6PD deficiency — test before prescribing.

entries.mechanism: Atovaquone disrupts mitochondrial electron transport; proguanil inhibits dihydrofolate reductase.
entries.uses: Malaria chemoprophylaxis, chosen by destination resistance pattern.
entries.cautions: Mefloquine causes vivid dreams and neuropsychiatric effects; atovaquone-proguanil well tolerated but expensive.

entries.mechanism: Blocks two steps in parasite folate synthesis.
entries.uses: Intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy and infancy; seasonal chemoprevention.
entries.cautions: Severe cutaneous reactions; widespread resistance limits curative use.

entries.mechanism: Bind parasite beta-tubulin, blocking glucose uptake and microtubule assembly.
entries.uses: Threadworm, roundworm, hookworm, whipworm; hydatid and neurocysticercosis (high dose).
entries.cautions: Generally well tolerated; marrow suppression with prolonged high-dose use; avoid in first trimester.

entries.mechanism: Opens glutamate-gated chloride channels present in invertebrates but not mammals, paralysing the parasite.
entries.uses: Onchocerciasis, strongyloidiasis, scabies, lymphatic filariasis.
entries.cautions: A transformative public-health drug; Mazzotti reaction from dying microfilariae; severe encephalopathy with heavy Loa loa burden.

entries.mechanism: Increases parasite membrane permeability to calcium, causing paralysis and tegument damage.
entries.uses: Schistosomiasis; tapeworm; liver fluke (clonorchiasis, opisthorchiasis — relevant across Southeast Asia).
entries.cautions: Abdominal pain, dizziness; single-dose treatment.

entries.mechanism: Alters microfilarial surface making them susceptible to host immune clearance.
entries.uses: Lymphatic filariasis; loiasis; tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.
entries.cautions: Severe reactions from dying parasites; contraindicated in onchocerciasis.

entries.mechanism: Pyrantel and levamisole depolarise nematode muscle; niclosamide uncouples tapeworm oxidative phosphorylation; triclabendazole targets fluke tubulin.
entries.uses: Roundworm and hookworm; tapeworm; fascioliasis (triclabendazole).
entries.cautions: Levamisole causes agranulocytosis; niclosamide acts only in the gut lumen.

entries.mechanism: Reductive activation inside anaerobic protozoa fragments DNA.
entries.uses: Amoebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis.
entries.cautions: Alcohol reaction; metallic taste.

entries.mechanism: Act only within the gut lumen to clear cyst carriage after tissue infection is treated.
entries.uses: Eradication of intestinal amoebic cysts.
entries.cautions: Ineffective against tissue invasion — must follow, not replace, metronidazole.

entries.mechanism: Blocks parasite folate synthesis at two steps; folinic acid is given to protect human marrow.
entries.uses: Toxoplasmosis, especially cerebral toxoplasmosis in HIV.
entries.cautions: Marrow suppression — always co-prescribe folinic acid; severe skin reactions.

entries.mechanism: Binds parasite DNA and interferes with several enzyme systems.
entries.uses: Pneumocystis pneumonia (second-line); early-stage African trypanosomiasis; leishmaniasis.
entries.cautions: Hypotension, hypoglycaemia then hyperglycaemia from pancreatic islet toxicity, nephrotoxicity.

entries.mechanism: Disrupts parasite membrane lipid metabolism and induces apoptosis-like death; the first effective oral treatment for visceral leishmaniasis.
entries.uses: Visceral and cutaneous leishmaniasis.
entries.cautions: Teratogenic with contraception required for months; GI intolerance.

entries.mechanism: Prodrugs reduced to trivalent antimony, which inhibits parasite glycolysis and trypanothione metabolism.
entries.uses: Leishmaniasis where newer agents are unavailable.
entries.cautions: Cardiotoxicity with QT prolongation, pancreatitis, hepatitis; long painful injection courses.

entries.mechanism: Generate reactive metabolites that damage trypanosomal DNA and protein.
entries.uses: Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis).
entries.cautions: Severe rash, peripheral neuropathy, weight loss; prolonged courses with poor completion rates.

entries.mechanism: Oral treatment effective in both stages of sleeping sickness — removing the need for lumbar puncture and arsenical infusion.
entries.uses: Human African trypanosomiasis.
entries.cautions: Neutropenia, vomiting; a major advance over melarsoprol.

entries.mechanism: Melarsoprol is an arsenical; suramin blocks parasite glycolytic enzymes; eflornithine inhibits ornithine decarboxylase.
entries.uses: Human African trypanosomiasis by stage and species.
entries.cautions: Melarsoprol causes a reactive encephalopathy fatal in roughly 5% — a treatment that itself kills, retained only because the disease is worse.

entries.mechanism: Disrupts arthropod sodium channels, causing paralysis.
entries.uses: Scabies (5% cream); head lice (1% lotion).
entries.cautions: Itch persists for weeks after successful treatment — warn patients so they do not re-treat unnecessarily. Treat all household contacts simultaneously.

entries.mechanism: Malathion inhibits parasite cholinesterase; benzyl benzoate is directly toxic to mites.
entries.uses: Scabies and head lice, especially where permethrin resistance exists.
entries.cautions: Benzyl benzoate stings badly on excoriated skin and is poorly tolerated in children.

entries.mechanism: Invertebrate chloride channel opening.
entries.uses: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies; resistant head lice; institutional outbreaks.
entries.cautions: Repeat dosing needed as it does not kill eggs.

entries.mechanism: Chemically cross-links DNA strands so the cell cannot divide; activated in the liver.
entries.uses: Lymphoma, leukaemia, breast, sarcoma; severe autoimmune disease and vasculitis.
entries.cautions: Haemorrhagic cystitis from the metabolite acrolein — prevented with mesna and hydration; marrow suppression; infertility; secondary malignancy.

entries.mechanism: As cyclophosphamide, with more acrolein produced per dose.
entries.uses: Sarcoma, testicular and paediatric tumours.
entries.cautions: Mandatory mesna; a distinctive encephalopathy from chloroacetaldehyde, reversed with methylthioninium chloride.

entries.mechanism: DNA cross-linking; melphalan is used at marrow-ablative doses before transplant.
entries.uses: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, myeloma, follicular lymphoma.
entries.cautions: Prolonged myelosuppression; secondary leukaemia; melphalan mucositis.

entries.mechanism: DNA cross-linking with marked stem-cell toxicity.
entries.uses: Conditioning before haematopoietic stem cell transplant.
entries.cautions: Pulmonary fibrosis (“busulfan lung”); veno-occlusive disease; seizures — prophylaxis given.

entries.mechanism: Methylate guanine, causing mismatch and strand breaks; temozolomide crosses the blood-brain barrier.
entries.uses: Hodgkin lymphoma, melanoma; glioblastoma (temozolomide).
entries.cautions: Severe emesis; temozolomide benefit depends on MGMT methylation status; procarbazine is a weak MAOI with a disulfiram-like alcohol reaction.
